The Supreme Court before it stood apart

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1592 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Political Supreme Court: A Forgotten History by Rachel A.
  • In her excellent upcoming book, The Political Supreme Court: A Forgotten History, professor Rachel Shelden closes with Chief Justice John Roberts’ insistence that “you don’t want the political branches telling you what the law is,” and that public opinion should not guide the court’s decisions.
  • That will likely sound quite familiar: it is how we have come to think about the Supreme Court.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Political Supreme Court: A Forgotten History by Rachel A. Shelden (The University of North Carolina Press).

In her excellent upcoming book, The Political Supreme Court: A Forgotten History, professor Rachel Shelden closes with Chief Justice John Roberts’ insistence that “you don’t want the political branches telling you what the law is,” and that public opinion should not guide the court’s decisions.

That will likely sound quite familiar: it is how we have come to think about the Supreme Court. But Shelden’s history highlights that the 19th century court and the way Americans perceived it were very different. Indeed, the modern idea of the detached judge, the justice as apolitical “umpire,” is not nearly as originalist as we tend to assume.

Industry observers note that shelden opens with Abraham Lincoln arguing before the court in 1849. The court that Lincoln and his fellow members of the bar knew was not the marble institution, removed from ordinary political life, that we picture today. For example, the justices “rode circuit.” Each was assigned a region, generally the part of the country from which he hailed and in which he traveled through to preside over federal trial courts. This brought the justices into regular contact with local lawyers, officials, and communities.

According to recent reports, shelden calls this “judicial representation”: the idea that a justice would bring a region’s perspective to the court because he knew the people he impliedly represented. Although today’s justices are assigned to a circuit, typically the circuit to which they have ties geographically, the concept is now decidedly different; except at certain prescheduled events, justices no longer directly communicate with the people in that circuit as part of their duties, but handle applications from it in the corridors of the marble palace. “Judicial representation” is most definitely no longer a thing.

But this just scratches the surface of the differences that Shelden lays out. In the 19th century, the justices were active participants in the political debates of their time, in ways that today would not only be grounds for profound criticism but even potential impeachment.

Sources indicate that chief Justice John Marshall was himself an active participant in such discourse. In 1800, before becoming chief, Marshall began contributing to the Washington Federalist, a newspaper established to support President John Adams and later oppose Thomas Jefferson. Marshall’s involvement was so extensive that he became known as the brains behind the paper. Nor did his appointment to the court entirely sever his connection to it. Elias Caldwell, the Supreme Court’s clerk during Marshall’s tenure, subsequently became its proprietor. The paper remained staunchly Federalist under Caldwell’s leadership, regularly attacking the Jefferson administration’s policies as unconstitutional.

Sources indicate that marshall’s political opponents suspected that he continued to exert considerable influence behind the scenes at the Washington Federalist even as chief justice, directing those attacks. Indeed, the Philadelphia Aurora, a newspaper aligned with Jefferson, described Caldwell as “a creature of John Marshall, chief justice.” Shelden casts doubt on Caldwell’s denial of Marshall’s involvement. And given that Caldwell was Marshall’s own clerk at the Supreme Court, you can understand the skepticism.

In a recent development, justice William Johnson provides another example. In 1823, Johnson ruled (in his lower-court circuit-riding role) that South Carolina’s Negro Seamen Act, which authorized the detention of free Black sailors arriving in Charleston, violated the Constitution. Local officials were furious and refused to publish his opinion in the newspapers. So Johnson took his argument directly to the public, putting his opinion in a pamphlet that was circulated around the country, and then supporting the decision via pseudonymously authored op-eds that submitted his interpretation of the Constitution was correct.

Nor were the justices’ newspaper writings limited to defending their decisions. In 1848, Justice John McLean published letters addressing such political issues as the national bank, taxation, infrastructure, and the Mexican-American War, all while his supporters were encouraging him to pursue the presidency.

And in 1859, Justice John Catron publicly opposed proposed Tennessee legislation that would have enslaved free Black residents who remained in the state. Catron used his connections at the Nashville Union and American to publish a letter criticizing the legislation. The newspaper’s editors attacked his position, producing a public back-and-forth in its pages. Catron’s letter was even reprinted in Missouri, where similar legislation was under consideration. Tennessee ultimately rejected the proposal, and Shelden suggests Catron’s intervention may have mattered.

To put this in perspective, such actions would be akin to Justice Clarence Thomas writing an opinion piece in The Wall Street Journal defending the Republican Party’s position on disputed legislation, or Justice Elena Kagan publishing an article in The Fresh York Times supporting a Democratic president’s legislative agenda.

Yet the justices’ political involvement went well beyond expressing opinions publicly. Some actually ran for elected office while continuing to serve on the court.

Shelden recounts the example of Justice Smith Thompson, who accepted the nomination for governor of New York in 1828 while a justice. Thompson ultimately lost to Martin Van Buren by more than 30,000 votes. After losing the election, Thompson simply continued serving on the court, where he remained for another 15 years.

It has been revealed that justice McLean, meanwhile, was discussed as a potential presidential candidate in the 1830s, with political allies contemplating his nomination even as he continued hearing cases. Indeed, both McLean and his colleague, Justice Levi Woodbury, would later emerge as presidential contenders in 1848.

Sources indicate that justice William Johnson, appointed by President Thomas Jefferson, actually won election as a commissioner of the poor in Charleston Neck, South Carolina, in 1826. In this role, he exercised authority over local taxation, patronage, and public resources. Johnson held this elected position, and won reelection, while continuing to serve on the Supreme Court.

Recent findings suggest that again, by way of comparison, imagine Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson declaring herself a candidate for the 2028 presidential election – while continuing to decide cases and write opinions. Or contemplate Justice Neil Gorsuch simultaneously holding an elected local government office with taxing authority.

In a recent development, just as notable was the willingness of justices to involve themselves directly in the work of the other branches of government. In doing so, they corresponded with presidents and members of Congress about public policy. They even offered advice on legislation and, in some instances, helped craft it.

According to recent reports, during Reconstruction, Chief Justice Salmon Chase pressed President Andrew Johnson on Black suffrage and used his political relationships to influence Reconstruction policy. For his part, just a few years earlier, Justice John Campbell of Alabama sought to influence President-elect Lincoln to concern a public statement reassuring Southern moderates that his administration would not interfere with slavery in their states. Campbell even offered to publish a letter in his own name, as a citizen of Alabama, to help create an occasion for Lincoln to make such a statement.

When Lincoln declined to act, Campbell turned to President James Buchanan. He urged Buchanan to send commissioners to the secession conventions to persuade the delegates to preserve the Union. Campbell’s efforts ultimately failed. But consider what he was doing: a sitting Supreme Court justice was privately advising both an incoming and an outgoing president about how to address the most consequential political crisis in the nation’s history.

Now imagine Chief Justice John Roberts privately consulting with President Donald Trump about birthright citizenship, or Justice Sonia Sotomayor advising former President Joe Biden about his unconstitutional student loan forgiveness program and how it could be fixed.

In the dénouement of the book, Shelden traces how the political world of the justices changed as the 19th century drew to a close. Circuit riding ended, the legal profession grew more formal, and the court became more centered in Washington. As the country marked the Constitution’s centennial, lawyers and judges helped tell a new story of the court, one that made political detachment seem like some sort of longstanding tradition. (To be fair, this did not bring such political involvement to an immediate end.).

Sources indicate that if I have one criticism of Shelden’s otherwise excellent work, it is that she doesn’t explore this transformation in nearly the same depth as she does the earlier history. How, exactly, did the justices (and their fellow Americans) come to accept a view of the court so different from the one they had held for much of the 19th century, and which we hold today? That is a fascinating question in its own right, and perhaps the worthy subject of a follow-up volume.

Industry observers note that regardless, Shelden’s history offers a challenge to today’s justices, as well as to proponents and critics of the modern court. Nineteenth-century justices participated much more freely in political life, while today’s justices insist that they must stand apart from politics, even as many Americans cast a dubious side eye upon that claim. Was it better when justices did not deny the political world they inhabited and were a part of? And can the way we look at the court, and the way the justices see themselves, change again? I don’t think the answers are obvious. But Shelden’s book made clear to me that a reflexive dismissal of such questions is based more on historical ignorance than any fixed tradition of the Supreme Court as appearing apolitical.

Mark Miller directs Environment and Natural Resources litigation at Pacific Legal Foundation.

According to recent reports, recommended Citation: Mark Miller, The Supreme Court before it stood apart, SCOTUSblog (Nov. 18, 2026, 10:00 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/11/the-supreme-court-before-it-stood-apart/.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that coinMarketCap is hiring a Head of Research to turn CMC data into research that institutions, media and partners trust and pay for. This is a senior, hands-on role reporting to the CMO.

CMC is the most referenced price and market data source in crypto. Our research already reaches millions each month through reports like our Monthly Exchange Report, Asset Watch and Market Pulse, and is cited by Bloomberg, WSJ, Forbes and Fortune. The next step is different. We are building CMC into a data platform for crypto, tokenized assets and broader markets, and research is how we prove the quality of that data to the people who buy it.

Sources indicate that you will own our research agenda end to end: what we publish, how rigorous it is, and how it supports our enterprise data business. You will also be the senior voice on sensitive market analysis for CMC and its partners.

Set and run the research roadmap, from recurring flagships (monthly exchange report, weekly market and asset coverage) to deep dives on exchanges, tokenized assets, RWAs and market structure.

Build institutional grade research that showcases CMC data to banks, funds, data buyers and enterprise API clients, working closely with our API and BD teams on what buyers need.

Own methodology and data integrity: define how we measure volume, liquidity, flows and reserves, document it, and make sure every published number holds up to scrutiny.

Lead research on sensitive or fast moving market events, balancing speed, neutrality and accuracy, and handle review requests from partners with sound judgement.

Be a credible public face for CMC research with tier one media, on panels and in interviews.

Manage and develop a small research team, at the moment one research analyst, and use AI and automation to scale output without lowering quality.

Partner with marketing, editorial and product to turn research into formats people actually read and share, from long form reports to charts and short social posts.

7+ years in research or data analysis, with at least 3 in crypto or digital asset markets.

A track record of published, data heavy research that institutions or serious media rely on.

Deep understanding of market structure: exchanges, spot and derivatives, liquidity, onchain flows and proof of reserves.

Strong quantitative skills and hands on data work (SQL or Python, APIs, large datasets).

Excellent written English and the judgement to present sensitive findings neutrally and accurately.

Experience leading or mentoring analysts.

Background at a crypto data provider, an institutional research desk or a TradFi data business.

Understanding of how data is packaged and sold to institutions (licensing, enterprise feeds, research subscriptions).

Knowledge of tokenized assets, RWAs or traditional market data.

Existing relationships with tier one financial and crypto media.

Comfort using AI tools to automate data pulls and drafts.

Mandarin, given our close work with Chinese speaking partners and media.

    • Pinellas County Circuit Judge Joseph A.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Lawyer Steven Cozzi, 41, who worked for Blanchard Law, a small law firm in Largo, Florida, went missing in 2023. Dr. Tomasz Kosowski of Florida was convicted of killing Cozzi and sentenced to death Friday. (Photo courtesy of the Largo Police Department).

    A Florida judge has sentenced a prominent plastic surgeon to death for the murder of a “beloved” lawyer who went missing in 2023, saying the doctor committed the crime in a “cold, calculated and premeditated manner.”.

    Pinellas County Circuit Judge Joseph A. Bulone handed down the death sentence Friday to Dr. Tomasz Kosowski of Florida, who was convicted in September of murdering attorney Steven Cozzi, 41, whom he faced in a contentious lawsuit, Law360 reports.

    According to recent reports, prosecutors said Cozzi was last seen entering the restroom of his law office in Largo, Florida, in March 2023. Surveillance video allegedly captured Kosowski walking into the law office’s main entrance on the morning that Cozzi went missing, showing the surgeon carrying a backpack and a large box. About two hours later, the video shows him walking out of the building with a different clothes and pulling a large cart covered with a red blanket.

    Cozzi, described as a “beloved” person, worked for Blanchard Law, a small law firm specializing in business litigation, bankruptcies and contract disputes. At the time of his disappearance, Cozzi was representing a defendant being sued by Kosowski over medical billing disputes. His body was never found.

    #147015. Five major complications that may still make it onto this term’s oral argument docket

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2665 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Five major complications that may still make it onto this term’s oral argument docket

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2665 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that time is running out for the justices to add cases to this term’s oral argument docket.
    • According to recent reports, but despite being short on time, the justices are not short on major petitions for review.
    • It has been revealed that before we explore some of the major challenges pending before the Supreme Court, let me first offer a brief refresher on how a petition for review makes it to the oral argument docket.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that time is running out for the justices to add cases to this term’s oral argument docket. Under the Supreme Court’s typical briefing schedule, a case must be granted by mid-January to be briefed in time for the final argument session, which begins this term on April 19.

    According to recent reports, but despite being short on time, the justices are not short on major petitions for review. Over the next two months, they will likely consider petitions addressing such high-profile issues as the Trump administration’s ban on transgender servicemembers, state laws requiring Ten Commandments displays in public school classrooms, and the regulation of prediction markets like Kalshi.

    It has been revealed that before we explore some of the major challenges pending before the Supreme Court, let me first offer a brief refresher on how a petition for review makes it to the oral argument docket. (For more on this process, read law professor Stephen Wermiel’s SCOTUSblog column from last week.).

    According to recent reports, litigants file a petition for review, also known as a petition for certiorari, at the Supreme Court when they want the justices to review a lower court ruling against them. In their petition, they lay out, among other things, their views on why the ruling was wrong and why the glitch is worthy of the justices’ attention.

    Recent findings suggest that after a petition is filed, the litigants that prevailed before the lower court (known as the respondents) have 30 days to respond, although they may ask for additional time. Sometimes, they file a brief in which they agree that the Supreme Court should take up the matter, but it’s far more common for respondents to file a brief in opposition, in which they explain why they believe the lower court’s ruling was correct and why the dispute does not warrant Supreme Court review.

    Once this brief has been filed – or once the respondent has formally waived its right to file such a brief (although the court may request one) – the court will schedule the petition for consideration at one of the justices’ private conferences. There are at least two such conferences every month during the term, and the court unveils in advance when these meetings will take place and when it will distribute the petitions assigned to each conference to the justices’ chambers.

    The court typically places a petition on a conference list at least 14 days after the response brief was filed. By counting 14 days from the response deadline and then consulting the distribution schedule, one can then (usually) predict the conference at which the justices will first consider a petition. (It should be noted, however, that the court sometimes delays consideration of a petition without explanation, interfering with court watchers’ predictive powers.).

    For a petition to make it to the oral argument docket, at least four of the nine justices need to vote to grant review. But the court rarely announces that a petition has been granted after the first conference at which it’s considered, likely because the court needs extra time to verify the details of the case. Instead, successful petitions are almost always relisted at least once, which means the justices take a second look at them during a successive conference. For this reason, the earliest a court watcher can expect to learn that a petition has been granted is generally after the second conference to which it’s assigned.

    Once a case is granted, litigants must file briefs on the merits, a process that takes at least three months under the court’s standard briefing schedule. That’s why a case must be granted by mid-January in order to be argued during the current term (unless the court adopts an expedited briefing schedule, which is a story for another day).

    Without further ado, here’s a look at five high-profile issues that have a shot at being taken up by the justices before that mid-January deadline.

    Ban on transgender servicemembers.

    One week after President Donald Trump returned to the White House in January 2025, he signed an executive order that required Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth to impose a ban “on individuals with gender dysphoria” – that is, distress based on a mismatch between an individual’s gender identity and biological sex. The next month, the Department of Defense issued a policy that generally disqualifies anyone who either has gender dysphoria or has undergone medical interventions to treat gender dysphoria from serving in the military.

    According to recent reports, this ban on transgender servicemembers led to a number of legal challenges, including a dispute that arrived on the Supreme Court’s interim docket in April 2025, United States v. Shilling. On May 6, 2025, the court granted the Trump administration’s request to pause an order from a federal judge in Washington state that had prevented implementation of the policy anywhere in the country.

    It has been revealed that shilling is now pending before the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit. A separate but related case, United States v. Talbott, has been appealed to the Supreme Court. Talbott involves a group of transgender people who either presently serve or want to serve in the U.S. military. After the Trump administration put the service ban in place, they went to federal court in Washington, D.C., contending that the policy violates their constitutional right to equal treatment by the government.

    Sources indicate that in March 2025, a federal judge in D.C. granted the challengers’ request to put the policy on hold, but the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit paused that ruling. A divided three-judge panel of the D.C. Circuit upheld part of the district court’s order in a June 2026 ruling, deciding that, while the case is ongoing, the Trump administration may not enforce its ban against the 28 current servicemembers involved. (However, the D.C. Circuit did not finalize that ruling until this week, after considering arguments over whether it should be implemented during the government’s appeal.).

    U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer appealed the D.C. Circuit’s ruling to the Supreme Court in late August, urging the justices to address the constitutionality of the ban on transgender servicemembers. He described the lower court decision as “gravely erroneous” and asserted that “[t]he authority of the U.S. military to determine who may serve in the Nation’s armed forces is a matter of exceptional importance.”.

    On Nov. 2, the challengers filed their brief in opposition and encouraged the Supreme Court to deny the petition. They emphasized that the D.C. Circuit issued a narrow preliminary injunction, not a broad final judgment, and that the record below is not yet developed.

    According to recent reports, as expected under the timeline discussed above, this petition was included on the conference list that was distributed on Tuesday, for the justices’ private conference on Dec. 4. If Talbott is relisted after the Dec. 4 conference, it will be considered again on Dec. 11 and could possibly be granted that day.

    It has been revealed that this week marks 46 years since the Supreme Court in Stone v. Graham struck down a Kentucky statute requiring a copy of the Ten Commandments to be posted in public school classrooms, holding that the law violated the First Amendment’s establishment clause. The justices have an opportunity to revisit that 1980 ruling this term if they take up challenges to similar policies in Texas and Louisiana.

    In a recent development, nathan v. Alamo Heights Independent School District is a challenge to the Texas law by a group of families with children in the state’s public schools. They contend that, in upholding the law, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit “flouted this Court’s binding precedents and gutted the religious-freedom rights of public-school children and parents.”.

    In a recent development, last week, Texas filed a brief in opposition to the petition, urging the justices to leave the 5th Circuit’s ruling in place. Among other arguments, the state notes that Texas’ incoming Democratic attorney general “has publicly stated that he ‘will not defend’ the challenged law” and contends that the matter will benefit from “further percolation in the lower courts.”.

    In a recent development, in addition to upholding Texas’ law, the 5th Circuit vacated preliminary injunctions preventing implementation of a similar policy in Louisiana. Despite this win, Louisiana filed a “conditional petition” with the Supreme Court in Brumley v. Roake, anticipating that the ACLU, which represents the challengers in both the Texas and Louisiana cases, would only appeal Nathan and telling the court that it should not review Texas’ law without also considering Louisiana’s law.

    In a recent development, in a separate case, Dier v. Landry, a Louisiana teacher, Christopher Dier, also asked the justices to consider whether Louisiana’s policy violates the establishment clause, but his case is complicated by a question of whether the fact that he filed his challenge before the law was implemented means it was not “ripe.” In its brief in opposition, Louisiana repeated the arguments it made in its conditional petition in Roake, asserting that the justices should grant one or both of the Louisiana cases if it grants review in the Texas case.

    In a recent development, because Texas’ response in Nathan and Louisiana’s response in Dier were filed on Nov. 10, these petitions will likely be considered by the justices for the first time at their Dec. 11 conference. That is the second and final conference in December, so it will be early January before the petitions could be considered a second time and potentially granted.

    As I previously reported for SCOTUSblog, immigration complications dominate this term’s oral argument docket. The court is weighing, among other things, the Trump administration’s practice of deporting noncitizens to countries not identified in their removal orders, its policy of detaining noncitizens without the opportunity for bond hearings, and its suspension of asylum.

    And there may be more immigration disputes to come. The justices are expected to soon consider Trump v. Suri and Khalil v. Trump, which address federal trial courts’ authority to review the legality of immigration detentions.

    Suri and Khalil, which involve Georgetown University scholar Badar Khan Suri and Columbia graduate Mahmoud Khalil, respectively, stem from the Trump administration’s push to deport students and academics because of their support for Palestine. Suri and Khalil were detained as part of this push, and while their deportation proceedings were ongoing, they challenged the legality of their detention in federal trial courts, alleging First Amendment violations. Both men prevailed before district courts, which ordered their release on bail. But while the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit upheld the decision in Suri’s case, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit ruled that the district court did not have the authority to consider Khalil’s challenges.

    Recent findings suggest that both cases have now been appealed to the Supreme Court, and they raise essentially the same question: Do federal trial courts have the power to consider a noncitizen’s challenge to his or her detention, or are such claims barred by federal immigration law, which generally requires all challenges “arising from” deportation proceedings or the decision to begin such proceedings to go first to a federal appeals court? In the government’s petition in Suri, Sauer told the justices that it may be best to grant review in both cases, because that approach “would guard against the possibility that either case might become moot (for example, due to the alien’s departure).”.

    The responses to these petitions are due on Friday. The court’s case distribution schedule indicates that they likely will be considered by the justices for the first time at their private conference on Jan. 8.

    Regulation of prediction markets.

    The rise of prediction markets like Kalshi and Polymarket has fueled a fierce legal battle between the companies operating the markets, state gambling regulators, and the federal government. The question at the center of the dispute is whether the prediction markets are subject to state gambling laws, or if, instead, they should answer only to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, the federal agency that regulates contract markets.

    According to recent reports, several federal courts of appeals have ruled on this question in recent months, and others are presently considering it. In Flaherty v. KalshiEX, LLC, New Jersey asks the Supreme Court to review a 3rd Circuit ruling in favor of Kalshi, which bars the state from enforcing gambling laws against the company. Robinhood Derivatives, LLC v. Dreitzer and North American Derivatives Exchange, Inc., dba Crypto.com v. Nevada are appeals of rulings by the 9th Circuit that reached the opposite conclusion: that contracts offered by prediction markets are not “swaps” and that, as a result, the CFTC does not have an exclusive right to regulate them.

    All of the parties involved agree that the stakes are high, urging the Supreme Court to get involved now and bring a resolution to the still-building surge of litigation.

    The responses to these three prediction market petitions are due on Dec. 7. The cases will likely then be distributed to the justices for consideration at the Jan. 8 conference.

    Judicial authority and other Trump cases.

    According to recent reports, in its June 2025 ruling in Trump v. CASA, the Supreme Court held that federal courts generally lack the authority to matter universal or nationwide injunctions blocking the government from enforcing a law or policy anywhere in the country. The ruling was significant, but it did not necessarily foreclose all forms of broad relief, as the Trump administration makes clear in Department of Health and Human Services v. Texas Medical Association, a petition it filed in October.

    It has been revealed that after CASA, lower courts have continued “to universally vacate agency rules under the Administrative Procedure Act,” the federal law governing administrative agencies, according to the petition. In so doing, Sauer wrote, they “re-create many of the same problems posed by universal injunctions.” He urged the justices to take up Texas Medical Association and “return the lower courts to their proper role under the APA” by making it clear “that relief should ordinarily be party-specific, not universal by default.”.

    Recent findings suggest that the case began as a group of challenges from the Texas Medical Association, a hospital, and four air ambulance companies to a 2022 law aimed at protecting patients from surprise medical bills. These challengers have until Dec. 14 to respond to the Trump administration’s petition.

    Recent findings suggest that that deadline means this petition likely won’t be considered by the justices until their Jan. 15 conference at the earliest. As noted above, cases typically need to be granted by mid-January to be argued during the current term, although the court sometimes adjusts the standard briefing schedule if it wants to add cases after the typical cut-off. The bottom line is that Department of Health and Human Services v. Texas Medical Association faces a steeper path to this term’s oral argument docket than the previously discussed petitions.

    The justices are also expected to address several other notable filings involving Trump by mid-January, including cases involving the president’s attempt to revive his suit against Hillary Clinton over what he describes as “a coordinated scheme ... to undermine his candidacy and Presidency through fabricated accusations of Russian collusion”; Trump’s suit against CNN for, according to him, “falsely and maliciously portray[ing]” him “as a knowing liar” with regard to the 2020 election; and his appeal of a $83.3 million judgment against him in a defamation case brought by journalist E. Jean Carroll.

    While it may be difficult to predict which disputes will make it to the oral argument docket, it’s not hard to conclude that the justices are in for a busy two months.

    Kelsey Dallas is SCOTUSblog's managing editor and the primary author of the SCOTUStoday newsletter.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Most growth teams call themselves data-driven.
    • Sources indicate that we want to be part of the 0.1%: a company where AI doesn’t just help the growth team, it runs the growth loop.
    • Then it’s your chance to define a newly introduced category : The Operating System (OS) for Human Greatness Augmented with AI.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Most growth teams call themselves data-driven. They have a dashboard, an agency and a ChatGPT licence to write ad copy faster. That’s the 99%.

    Sources indicate that we want to be part of the 0.1%: a company where AI doesn’t just help the growth team, it runs the growth loop. Every day, on every channel.

    Then it’s your chance to define a newly introduced category : The Operating System (OS) for Human Greatness Augmented with AI.

    According to recent reports, science-backed. Design-led. AI-powered. Global.

    In a recent development, we’re not looking for someone who only advises on what to test, we’re looking for someone who builds it. A hands-on Head of Growth who can ideate, write the copy, design the strategy and launch experiments directly.

    Our growth machine has to be able to:.

    1. Generate hypotheses. Read the signals (ad performance, webinar attendance, sales calls, objections, churn reasons, comments, competitors’ ads) and propose what to test next, with a cost and an expected impact.

    In a recent development, 2. Act across every tool. Not a chatbot in a tab: it reads and writes in our whole stack, from ad accounts to CRM, landing pages, webinars, email, social DMs and analytics.

    3. Hold the full context of Paradox. Our DNA, offers, voice, member stories, past campaigns and what they taught us, in one shared firm brain.

    Sources indicate that 4. Ship its hypotheses. Produce the hook, the ad cut, the page, the email sequence or the funnel variant, and put it live.

    5. Measure with real KPIs. Every test is tied to a number that matters (cost per qualified lead, show-up rate, close rate, CAC, payback, LTV), not to likes or reach.

    #147012. Latest Update: Calls for court packing fail the test of history

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1340 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: Calls for court packing fail the test of history

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1340 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Please note that SCOTUS Outside Opinions constitute the views of outside contributors and do not reflect the opinions of SCOTUSblog or its staff.
    • Recent findings suggest that as Democrats have taken control in Congress, we can expect calls for court packing to intensify.
    • Industry observers note that some of these calls come with superficially plausible justifications.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Please note that SCOTUS Outside Opinions constitute the views of outside contributors and do not reflect the opinions of SCOTUSblog or its staff.

    Recent findings suggest that as Democrats have taken control in Congress, we can expect calls for court packing to intensify. One especially prominent proposal has been to expand the court to 13 justices. In the last few months, we have seen former Vice President Kamala Harris say the Supreme Court should be increased to this number. In August, Rep. James Clyburn, a longtime Democratic leader in the House, endorsed this proposal on “Meet the Press.” Just in the past few weeks, Hillary Clinton noted the party “should seriously look at expanding the court while the Democrats are in power.” Potential presidential candidate Pete Buttigieg has advocated increasing the number of justices to 13 as well.

    Industry observers note that some of these calls come with superficially plausible justifications. Take Hillary Clinton’s proposal, for instance. “It used to be that you’d have one justice for each circuit,” Clinton explained. “We now have 13 circuits, we should have 13 justices.” Buttigieg has also argued for modifying the size of the court on that basis. But the symmetry argument is pretextual: It is no mere coincidence that the reintroduction of a one-to-one justice to circuit relationship under Democratic control would produce exactly the four seats needed to transform the current six-to-three conservative majority into a seven-to-six liberal one. Such a proposal then allows advocates to cover their desire for change to the court’s size in the language of a seemingly neutral principle.

    In a recent development, it is true that the Constitution doesn’t fix the number of justices. And changes to the court’s size have not always been made for partisan reasons. In many cases there have been administrative and logistical needs that made changes to the size of the court practically useful, and even necessary. For that reason, we do not oppose changing the court’s size as such. Rather, we only oppose court packing, which we define as changing the court’s size for partisan reasons.

    So how can one tell the difference?

    As we argue in a recent paper, and as already noted above, a key distinction when evaluating proposed changes to the court’s size is whether that change is constrained by some sort of even-handed principle or whether the change is driven by partisan advantage. Throughout American history, legitimate changes to the court’s size have answered practical problems, such as those accompanying the logistics of circuit-riding. A defining feature of court packing, by sharp contrast, is that it changes the court’s size primarily to benefit a particular political coalition without recourse to some prior rule or norm.

    According to recent reports, political coalitions can always claim a pretextual justification for adding justices, allowing the political benefit to be presented as secondary to pressing administrative reasons. But the stated rationale for a proposed change cannot be enough to legitimize the change. Instead, a legitimate proposal must respond to a genuine institutional need. The grounds for change must, in other words, predate the political conflict rather than be identified retroactively to manufacture a justification for changing the court’s size.

    Industry observers note that the 13-justice proposal, from this historical perspective, utterly fails the test. The one-circuit, one-justice rule previously existed because justices actually rode circuit, traveling to hear cases in the lower courts. In those days each new circuit needed a justice to staff it. As the country grew westward, Congress added justices to staff new circuits (one in 1807, two in 1837, one in 1863). While, admittedly, those changes benefited the party in power, few treated them as a way to assert partisan control over the court.

    Recent findings suggest that but circuit-riding ended more than a century ago. Today the number of circuits has no practical connection with the performance of the justices. For example, when Congress carved the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit out of the 8th in 1929, circuits first outnumbered justices, and Congress did not add a seat. Nor did it add one when it split the overburdened U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit to create the 11th in 1980, and there were not calls to do so. And when the specialized U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit was added as the 13th Circuit in 1982, no one argued for a corresponding increase to the court. Rather, arguments for reestablishing the proportionality between circuits and seats on the Supreme Court have resurfaced only now after a string of decisions particularly unpopular with Democrats (most notably Dobbs).

    Sources indicate that timing also reveals the motive behind these assertions. If the rationale for increasing the court’s size was merely or even primarily procedural and administrative, then there would be no reason to delay. But instead, as Clinton has stated, the court’s size should only be increased “while the Democrats are in power.” Nor, for that matter, have proponents named any administrative problem that four more justices would solve.

    Recent findings suggest that to clarify intentions let us explore a simple thought experiment. If Democrats believed the court needs four more justices, they could prove it by passing legislation to add two seats now, to be filled by President Donald Trump, and two more in 2029, to be filled by whoever wins the 2028 election. Accordingly, the court would get its 13 justices and achieve circuit symmetry. Democrats will undoubtedly not offer that deal, however, because under this scenario there would remain a three-seat conservative majority. This demonstrates, of course, that the case for 13 justices is not, in fact, about the number 13 at all – it is about who gets to appoint the four.

    Sources indicate that finally, history makes clear the consequences of changing the court’s size for partisan advantage. In 1801, lame-duck Federalists passed a law shrinking the court at its next vacancy in an attempt to deny Thomas Jefferson an appointment on it. The Republicans repealed this act, turning the judiciary into an object of partisan action and reaction, a conflict that culminated in the impeachment of Justice Samuel Chase in 1804. In 1866, Republicans shrank the court by attrition to keep Andrew Johnson from making appointments, defeating his pending nominee and leaving the circuit courts understaffed in the process. In 1869, with Republican Ulysses Grant elected, Congress set the number of justices at nine, contracting the court under a hostile president and expanding it under an allied one. Grant’s appointees then helped reverse a major ruling on paper money, a change that could arguably be seen as the product of Congress’ manipulation rather than constitutional reasoning.

    The allure of court packing for partisan purposes will only continue to grow over the next two years. With Trump in office until January 2029, a Democratic Congress cannot expand the court on its own, so court packing will likely become a standard talking point leading to the 2028 Democratic presidential primary and the subsequent general election. As that debate continues to unfold, voters should remember one question to ask of these proposals: is the proposed change answering a legitimate, administrative problem with the court’s functioning, or is it a partisan reaction to the rulings themselves? Only the first should be understood as legitimate grounds to consider changes to the size of the nation’s highest court. Anything else risks escalating partisan retribution and destruction of the judiciary’s ability to act independently, a role that John Adams rightly identified as foundational for “the stability of government, in all its branches, the morals of the people, and every other blessing of society and social institutions.”.

    According to recent reports, jordan J. Ballor is executive director of First Liberty’s Center for Religion, Culture & Democracy.

    Logan Tantibanchachai is a research fellow at First Liberty’s Center for Religion, Culture & Democracy.

    It has been revealed that then-White House press secretary Katie Zacharia speaks during a news briefing Oct. 13, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Photo by Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images).

    A former White House press secretary for President Donald Trump—whose tenure lasted five days in October—is facing an investigation by the State Bar of California after describing herself as a lawyer without being licensed to practice law.

    Katie Zacharia, who graduated with a JD from the Pepperdine University Rick J. Caruso School of Law in 2011, never passed the bar but has repeatedly referred to herself as a lawyer. A California code claims a candidate must have passed the bar exam to be called a lawyer.

    Zacharia has mentioned she worked as the outside counsel to the World Bank, an international financial institution, and as the general counsel for a conservative California nonprofit, according the Campaign for Accountability, a nonprofit government watchdog group.

    The Campaign for Accountability received a notice of the probe in a Thursday letter from the state bar and told the nonprofit that its complaint was assigned to an investigator and legal adviser.

    “Zacharia may have thought she was just playing a lawyer on TV, but by repeatedly holding herself out as an attorney on news programs, she was pretending to have authority she lacks,” noted Michelle Kuppersmith, the executive director of the Campaign for Accountability, in a statement Thursday.

    Katie Zacharia out as White House press secretary.

    New White House press secretary calls confusion over legal credentials misunderstanding.

    Is she or isn’t she? Trump’s new press secretary claims she took the bar—in China.

    Trump administration withdraws application to Supreme Court to block lower court ruling on protected status for Venezuelan nationals

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (610 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that originally published on Nov.
    • Recent findings suggest that the battle over the Temporary Protected Status program – which allows foreign nationals to remain in the United States and work here when they cannot safely return home – returned to the Supreme Court on Wednesday afternoon.
    • Then-DHS Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas designated Venezuela for the TPS program in 2021 and again in 2023.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that originally published on Nov. 18; updated with latest developments on Nov. 19 at 4:35 p.m.

    Recent findings suggest that the battle over the Temporary Protected Status program – which allows foreign nationals to remain in the United States and work here when they cannot safely return home – returned to the Supreme Court on Wednesday afternoon. Specifically, the Trump administration asked the justices to block a September 2025 ruling by a federal judge in San Francisco that kept the program in place for Venezuelan nationals. U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer told the court that if they do not act, the order by U.S. District Judge Edward Chen “will spring into effect, inflicting severe and immediate harm.”.

    Then-DHS Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas designated Venezuela for the TPS program in 2021 and again in 2023. In 2025, he announced that the program would be extended through October 2026. Mayorkas cited a “severe humanitarian emergency” resulting from the “severe political and economic crisis” in Venezuela as the reason for the designation.

    According to recent reports, after Mayorkas’ successor, Kristi Noem, confirmed her decisions to end Venezuela’s designation and its subsequent extension, a group representing TPS holders went to federal court in San Francisco to challenge those decisions. Chen set them aside, and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit upheld that ruling. In 2025, while that litigation was moving forward, the Supreme Court paused Chen’s order with regard to Venezuela, effectively clearing the way for the Trump administration to deport Venezuelan TPS beneficiaries while the case continued.

    In June 2026, in Mullin v. Doe, the Supreme Court ruled – in a pair of cases involving Haitian and Syrian TPS beneficiaries – that courts generally cannot review the Secretary of Homeland Security’s decision to designate or terminate a country under the TPS program. Relying on that decision, the Trump administration asked the court to send the Venezuelan TPS case back to the 9th Circuit for another look, which the court did in October of this year.

    It has been revealed that when the case returned to the 9th Circuit, Sauer told the justices, and the Supreme Court’s initial stay of Chen’s ruling expired, the court of appeals entered an administrative stay, which is due to expire on Nov. 20. “Absent judicial intervention between now and” then, Sauer wrote, “the Department of Homeland Security will have to resurrect TPS status for hundreds of thousands of Venezuelans after a nineteen-month hiatus.” Indeed, he noted, his office “has been informed that the government could be forced to immediately release into the country some 1800 or so Venezuelan aliens from detention.” And all of this would result, he continued, even though the Supreme Court has already “conclusively held in Doe” that the TPS statute bars courts from reviewing the DHS secretary’s decision to designate or end the designation of TPS.

    Recent findings suggest that on Thursday, the Trump administration withdrew its application. In a letter to Scott Harris, the clerk of the Supreme Court, Sauer explained that “a few hours after we filed our stay application, the court of appeals issued an order” extending its current administrative stay (and therefore keeping Chen’s ruling on hold) until seven days after it issues a decision. “Should the Ninth Circuit enter an adverse judgment,” Sauer added, “we intend to immediately return to this Court for additional relief.”.

    Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that after adding cases on President Donald Trump’s suspension of asylum for immigrants at the U.S.-Mexico border and the standard for securities-fraud lawsuits to the oral argument docket last Friday, the justices began this week by denying a number of notable petitions, including two DEI-related disputes. Then, on Wednesday, the Trump administration brought a familiar battle back to the Supreme Court’s interim docket, asking the court to address its effort to remove protected status from Venezuelan nationals. The administration withdrew that request on Thursday, however, citing a upcoming lower-court ruling.

    Finally, a few housekeeping notes:.

    On Thursday, the Supreme Court denied a request for a stay of execution from Thomas Overton, who was sentenced to death for killing Michael and Susan “Missy” MacIvor and their unborn child in 1991. Hours later, Overton was executed in Florida.

    Also on Thursday, the court denied a request for a stay of execution from Reinaldo Dennes, who was sentenced to death for the 1996 murder of Janos Szucs. Hours later, Dennes was executed in Texas.

    According to recent reports, on Wednesday, the battle over the Temporary Protected Status program – which allows foreign nationals to remain in the United States and work when they cannot return home – returned to the Supreme Court, as the Trump administration asked the justices to block a September 2025 district court ruling that kept the program in place for Venezuelan nationals. As noted above, the government withdrew that request on Thursday.

    According to recent reports, on Tuesday, the Supreme Court indicated that several notable petitions for review will be considered at the justices’ next private conference on Friday, December 4. The disputes address such challenges as the Trump administration’s ban on transgender servicemembers and its approach to appointing acting U.S. attorneys.

    The Supreme Court on Monday denied review in dozens of cases, including a clash between the Trump administration and University of California scholars over cuts to research funding; a California ophthalmologist’s challenge to diversity-related requirements for continuing medical education courses; and a dispute over Maryland’s ban on carrying firearms in “sensitive places.” It also invited the United States solicitor general to share the government’s views on a trio of cases brought against the Taliban by victims of terrorist attacks.

    The Supreme Court Building will be closed for Thanksgiving on Thursday, November 26, and Friday, November 27.

    The December argument session will begin on Monday, November 30. On Wednesday, December 2, the court will hear argument in Viramontes v. Cook County, on the constitutionality of AR-15 bans, at 10:00 a.m. EST. We will be live blogging that morning beginning at 9:30 a.m.

    Michael Phillis, Associated Press.

    In a petition for review filed earlier this month, the Trump administration asked the Supreme Court to weigh in on “its push to cut $16 billion in grants for a climate program, the largest grant cancellation case ever,” according to the Associated Press. “Democratic President Joe Biden’s administration awarded the money under a 2022 law to finance clean energy projects and accelerate the transition from fossil fuels,” but after President Donald Trump took office, the Environmental Protection Agency rescinded the grants. Groups that lost the money challenged this decision, and “[i]n August, a divided federal appeals court in Washington sided with the nonprofits and stated the administration improperly terminated the grants.” “The administration has been adamant that nothing requires them to make these grants to these groups.”.

    According to recent reports, on Thursday, U.S. District Judge Steven Merryday “allowed President Donald Trump to proceed with portions of his $15 billion defamation lawsuit against the New York Times and Penguin Random House LLC,” in which the president accuses the news outlet and publisher “of tarnishing his reputation with false stories about his business acumen before the 2024 presidential election,” according to Bloomberg. Merryday concluded that “Trump had sufficiently alleged ‘actual malice’ in connection with” seven “disputed statements, which requires showing that the authors and publishers knew the statements were false or recklessly disregarded whether they were false. It’s a high bar that must be met by public figures who sue for defamation, established by the Supreme Court decades ago to protect press freedoms.”.

    Nicholas Kristof, The New York Times.

    In a column for The New York Times, Nicholas Kristof described meeting with five men who were deported from the United States to South Sudan through a process known as “third-country removals” that has been embraced by the Trump administration and will soon be considered by the Supreme Court. The men, according to Kristof, “were nearly starving, can’t regularly communicate with their families or anyone else and don’t have any path to get to their home countries or, in the case of some of them, to ever see their American citizen children again.” “I hope the justices will take note of what has happened to those sent to South Sudan,” he wrote.

    In a post for his Substack, Ed Whelan reflected on the potential reasons why Judge Cornelia Kennedy of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 6th Circuit, who was once described by a senator as “probably the most exceptional woman judge in the country,” was passed over for a Supreme Court nomination in favor of “a virtual unknown, Sandra Day O’Connor,” amid President Ronald Reagans quest “to nominate the first female justice.” O’Connor likely benefitted from, among other things, having “a powerful advocate” in Chief Justice Warren Burger, who “energetically lobb[ied] for O’Connor with White House officials and evidently with Reagan himself.” A comparison between O’Connor and Kennedy “offers lessons about the pressures and incentives that shape a president’s selection of a Supreme Court nominee,” Whelan wrote.

    In a recent development, in a piece on the legacy of Judge Richard Posner, who died on November 10, The Economist celebrated his remarkable career, describing him as “a giant of American law.” Scholars told the publication that “Posner may prove more influential than many Supreme Court justices,” in large part because he wrote “more than 500 articles, 50 books and 3,300 judicial opinions on everything from the law and sex to how judges think” during his career. “We pay attention to the justices because their opinions matter, but very few of them have anything interesting or original to offer,” remarked Larry Kramer of the London School of Economics. “Dick Posner did.”.

    Recent findings suggest that on Thursday, the Trump administration withdrew its request for the Supreme Court to block a lower court ruling that would allow Venezuelan nationals to participate in the Temporary Protected Status program, noting that the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit has ensured the ruling will remain on hold. “Should the Ninth Circuit enter an adverse judgment,” wrote U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer, “we intend to immediately return to this Court for additional relief.”.

    Sources indicate that time is running out for the justices to add cases to this term’s oral argument docket. Despite being short on time, however, the justices are not short on major petitions for review. Over the next two months, they will likely consider petitions addressing such high-profile complications as the Trump administration’s ban on transgender servicemembers and state laws requiring Ten Commandments displays in public school classrooms.

    By Jordan J. Ballor & Logan Tantibanchachai.

    In a recent development, in a column for SCOTUSblog, Jordan J. Ballor and Logan Tantibanchachai reflected on Democrats’ recent embrace of court packing, which they “define as changing the court’s size for partisan reasons.” Such an approach to court reform “risks escalating partisan retribution and destruction of the judiciary’s ability to act independently,” they wrote.

    By César Cuauhtémoc García Hernández.

    Industry observers note that in his Immigration Matters column on Wednesday, César Cuauhtémoc García Hernández explored what Democrats’ success in the midterm elections could mean for a challenge to an Iowa law criminalizing certain immigration-related conduct, Bird v. Iowa Migrant Movement for Justice. Because Iowa’s Republican attorney general lost her reelection bid to a Democrat, it’s now unclear if the state will move forward with its defense of the law, “providing yet another reason why elections matter.”.

    Industry observers note that in his Courtly Observations column on Tuesday, Erwin Chemerinsky revisited the oral argument in St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy, during which several conservative justices appeared to suggest “that a law’s discriminatory effect against a religion should be a basis for striking it down.” Such an approach to free exercise would be at odds “with a half century of law under equal protection holding that disparate impact ... is not enough to prove discrimination,” Chemerinsky contended.

    Recent findings suggest that in her In the Interim column on Monday, Taraleigh Davis revisited comments made by Justice Samuel Alito this fall about the court’s emergency docket, including why it’s so busy these days. The data, according to Davis, “support part of what Alito remarked but complicate the rest.”.

    Sarah Isgur and David French discuss the nature of lame-duck confirmations after the showdown between Texas Sens. John Cornyn and Ted Cruz, journalists’ records, and weakening the presidential veto.

    Akhil Amar and Andy Lipka continue their discussion on the significance of and fallout from this month’s midterm elections.

    Recent findings suggest that the Closer Look in Friday editions is typically a judicial biography. This week, we cover Justice Levi Woodbury, who served on the court from 1845 to 1851.

    Being the first justice to attend law school and the first of two Upcoming Hampshire justices (the second being Justice David Souter) has not saved Justice Levi Woodbury’s reputation from “declin[ing] dramatically over the years,” as a “reputational study” of the justice published in the Journal of Supreme Court History put it.

    Woodbury was born in December 1789 in Francestown, New Hampshire. As the eldest son, he faced immense pressure to succeed and was “near obsessive” about his education, according to Oyez. He attended Atkinson Academy before enrolling at Dartmouth at 16, earning money teaching in the towns around Hanover to afford school.

    According to recent reports, woodbury then attended law school (the other justices had “read law” through apprenticeships or were self-taught), studying at Litchfield Law school in Connecticut. Per Oyez, however, his time there was brief: He rapidly came to the conclusion that he “did not enjoy [law school]” and apprenticed instead before being admitted to the bar in 1812.

    During the War of 1812, Woodbury drafted the Hillsborough Resolves, statements backing President James Madison’s decision to fight Britain (and arguing against Daniel Webster’s condemnation of the war). With this, Woodbury became “one of the few” Upcoming Englanders to support the War of 1812. While then clerking for the state Senate, Woodbury connected with Gov. William Plumer, who in 1816 appointed Woodbury, then 27, to the New Hampshire Superior Court (the state’s top court).

    Sources indicate that in 1823, the Latest Hampshire Democratic-Republicans faced “bitter factionalism within,” and a group of them (displeased with their caucus’ choice for governor) chose Woodbury as their nominee instead, helping him to become New Hampshire’s 15th governor by a significant margin. Woodbury’s attempt to reunite the party met with little success, however, and he was not reelected. Still, by 1825 Woodbury had become speaker of the state House and a U.S. senator and later chaired the Senate Committee on Commerce. During that time, Woodbury, who was sympathetic to President Andrew Jackson, supported the Indian Removal Act of 1830. He was subsequently appointed by Jackson in March 1831 as secretary of the Navy.

    In 1834, Jackson shifted Woodbury to the Treasury, where he denied entrusting federal money to the Second Bank of the United States (like his predecessor, Roger B. Taney), instead giving it to commercial banks. In that position, he also issued the Specie Circular, which directed federal land offices to accept “nothing except what is directed by the existing laws, viz, gold and silver, and in the proper cases Virginia land scrip,” but not paper money, for land purchases. The Circular is often cited as a “primary cause” of the Panic of 1837.

    According to recent reports, in 1841, Woodbury returned to the Senate rather than serve as chief justice of Newly introduced Hampshire’s Superior Court. After Justice Joseph Story died in September 1845, President James Polk nominated Woodbury as a recess appointment to the Supreme Court, and he was confirmed by the Senate that January.

    In 1847, Woodbury authored the court’s unanimous opinion in Jones v. Van Zandt, which upheld the Fugitive Slave Act of 1793 as constitutional. Oyez writes that although “[m]any thought this indicated a pro-slavery stance … really his vote was motivated by an appreciation for states’ rights and a fear that the constitution was being interpreted too liberally.” Yet whereas Justice John McLean wrote that “the Constitution treats slaves as persons,” Woodbury “repeatedly referr[ed] to enslaved people as ‘property.’” One anti-slavery paper wrote that “if there be a man in the United States utterly heartless on the subject of slavery, it is Levi Woodbury” and that “[w]e know of no opinion on record of any slaveholding court, so inhumane in tone and language, as the opinion of Judge Woodbury, declared in the Van Zandt case.”.

    In 1849’s Luther v. Borden, Woodbury was the only justice to dissent, concluding that Rhode Island’s statute establishing martial law was unconstitutional. Under such a law, he wrote, the “whole population” was “exposed … to be seized, without warrant or oath” and that “[b]y it, every citizen … exists with, a rope around his neck.” Woodbury likewise dissented in 1849’s Passenger Cases, which asked whether a tax could be imposed “upon alien passengers” arriving in the ports of New York and Massachusetts. Woodbury wrote that the commerce clause did not give the federal government exclusive immigration powers, and that states could tax immigrants after they arrived in the state ports.

    Woodbury also pursued his political ambitions while on the court. In 1848, John C. Calhoun noted – reportedly influenced by Woodbury’s decision in Van Zandt – that he “would run best in the South.” Woodbury campaigned for president, but his apparent efforts to appeal to both slavery and anti-slavery advocates hurt his candidacy, and Lewis Cass ultimately received the Democratic nomination.

    Although Woodbury “looked like a front-runner again for an 1852 nomination,” he died in 1851 in Portsmouth, Latest Hampshire, at age 61, and the nomination went to his former clerk, Franklin Pierce.

    CHIEF JUSTICE ROBERTS: “Just okay?”.

    • Nora is an editorial assistant at SCOTUSblog, based in Washington, D.C.

    In a recent development, in June 2023, the court decided Students for Fair Admissions, Inc. v. University of North Carolina, holding that race-conscious admissions at Harvard and the University of North Carolina violated the Constitution. Chief Justice John Roberts’ majority opinion in the case, along with Justice Brett Kavanaugh’s concurrence, cited Justice Sandra Day O’Connor’s 2003 prediction in Grutter v. Bollinger that “25 years from now, the use of racial preferences will no longer be necessary to further” student body diversity.

    But the justices did not account for one thing, according to Brooklyn Law School Professor Yuvraj Joshi: O’Connor’s later misgivings about that statement. In interviews with her biographer after she left the court, O’Connor acknowledged that the 25-year figure “may have been a misjudgment.” When asked for a upcoming estimate, she replied, “[t]here’s no timetable. You just don’t know.”.

    Nora is an editorial assistant at SCOTUSblog, based in Washington, D.C.

Even though you work from home, we try to ensure you always have colleagues alongside to coach and mentor you, and for the companionship of shared problem solving and pair programming. We don't generally work weekends and nights and we do enjoy good holidays but we also expect productive and intense engagement Monday to Friday.

This is a fantastic way to demonstrate and develop your skill in software, learn about a wide range of technologies, make a meaningful impact to open source, and see some very interesting new cities that you might never otherwise get to visit.

    SAN FRANCISCO (CN) â âI really don’t know what to do with this case,â Senior U.S. District Judge Maxine Chesney remarked Friday as a legal fight between Amazon and Perplexity AI returned to her court.

    By the end of the three-hour hearing, the Bill Clinton appointee had granted Perplexity’s request for a stay in discovery, saying it would keep costs down and give her time to consider a dismissal motion. Neither Amazon nor Perplexity immediately responded to requests for comment.

    Perplexity is the developer of Comet, an AI web browser capable of shopping on Amazon, including by comparing prices and reviews.

    Recent findings suggest that amazon argues the tool violates laws like the U.S. Computer Fraud and Abuse Act. Chesney previously found that Amazon would likely succeed on those arguments â then a Ninth Circuit panel rejected her findings, sending the case back to her court.

    Recent findings suggest that “It is the user who âaccessesâ Amazonâs computers with the help of the assistant,” U.S. Circuit Judge Milan Smith Jr., a George W. Bush appointee, wrote for the panel. A claim by Amazon under the California Comprehensive Computer Data Access and Fraud Act failed under the same logic.

    On Friday, Chesney asked Amazon and Perplexity how she should apply the panel’s ruling.

    Hagan Scotten, an attorney with the firm Hueston Hennigan who is representing Amazon, told the judge there were newly introduced facts that the appeals court had not considered.

    It has been revealed that A new version of Comet had been released since the panel’s decision, Scotten said. He also said Perplexity employees had tested versions of Comet on Amazon.

    Scotten also argued the panel did not fully understand how Comet works.

    Recent findings suggest that the judges, he said, mistakenly believed that Comet only shopped on Amazon when directed by a user to do so. In fact, he said, a user might simply ask Comet to buy an item, then the tool would go to Amazon without being “invited in.”.

    Representing Perplexity with the firm Quinn Emanuel, attorney Daniel Posner pushed back on Scotten’s claims, including the argument that facts had changed since the Ninth Circuit ruling.

    Recent findings suggest that comet cannot access Amazon itself, he said. Instead, a user must give the AI assistant access to their Amazon account.

    âThe user always directs the agent to do something," he said. “That is the underpinning of the Ninth Circuit ruling.”.

    According to recent reports, posner argued Amazon was “scraping the barrel” in an effort to save its case. He cited Amazon’s claims that Perplexity employees were accessing Amazon.
