    #147000. Criminal law is constitutional law

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2344 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Criminal law is constitutional law

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2344 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • With arguments over the Second Amendment and the Excessive Fines Clause on the near horizon, this column seeks to provide some tranquil and more generalized ideas – a moment of Thanksgiving holiday respite.
    • Winship – criminal law fundamentals are constitutional law.
    • Industry observers note that every criminal law class I have taught over 40 years, from 1L first semester through advanced criminal procedure or federal criminal law, has begun with the same case: 1970’s In re Winship.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    With arguments over the Second Amendment and the Excessive Fines Clause on the near horizon, this column seeks to provide some tranquil and more generalized ideas – a moment of Thanksgiving holiday respite. Whether you are a Supreme Court follower who usually shunts criminal law to the side, or an experienced criminal law reader who might enjoy some holiday dinner thoughts for your friends and family, this column seeks to demonstrate that much of criminal law is actually constitutional law – and perhaps show why that can be so interesting. To do so, I will scatter some examples from last term, drawn from my recently published Annual Review of the Supreme Court’s Term, Criminal Cases booklet. When explaining criminal law to your friends or just opining over Thanksgiving dinner, I’d like to show why your mantra should be “crim law is con law” and vice versa.

    Winship – criminal law fundamentals are constitutional law.

    Industry observers note that every criminal law class I have taught over 40 years, from 1L first semester through advanced criminal procedure or federal criminal law, has begun with the same case: 1970’s In re Winship. Even non-lawyers know from film and TV that the prosecution’s high burden for proof in a criminal case is beyond a reasonable doubt. But do they know that this is constitutionally required? And perhaps more interesting, that this standard is nowhere, textually, in that document?

    “[T]he Due Process Clause protects the accused against conviction except upon proof beyond reasonable doubt of every fact necessary to constitute the crime with which he is charged,” wrote Justice William Brennan Jr. for the Winship court. If only all Supreme Court decisions had such clear and succinct rule statements.

    Sources indicate that but why is this the rule? It is not found either in the body of the Constitution or in the Bill of Rights, which was adopted soon after the Constitution and focused largely on criminal law protections. Winship‘s answer: because that standard “dates back at least from our early years as a Nation,” “[i]t is now accepted in common law jurisdictions,” it is expressed “in many opinions of this Court,” and it has “long been assumed” to be “constitutionally required.” Thus history, tradition, and precedent support it. Perhaps most fundamentally, a high standard of proof, harder to satisfy than in civil law cases, is essential to fundamental fairness for the public as well as individuals charged with crimes. It is “indispensable to command the respect and confidence of the community” as well as “every individual” exposed to imprisonment. Or, as Justice John Harlan II wrote in an influential concurrence, this standard is “bottomed on a fundamental value determination of our society that it is far worse to convict an innocent man than to let a guilty man go free.”.

    According to recent reports, thus, a fundamental premise of criminal law, Winship, is constitutional law too. Moreover, and just by the way, Winship demonstrates that the “incorporation” theory of the 14th Amendment’s Due Process Clause (that is, applying the Bill of Rights to the states) is not limited to concepts stated expressly in the Bill of Rights itself – as “proof beyond a reasonable doubt” is not. Critics of non-textual constitutional rights – like privacy, a right to travel, a right to refuse medical treatment (like mask wearing?), or even a right to terminate a pregnancy – must confront the application of their literalist theory to proof beyond a reasonable doubt, too. For this reason, I also teach Winship in every constitutional law class.

    There are almost no crimes mentioned in the Constitution.

    In a recent development, this sometimes surprises 1L students (and others). But the goal of the Constitution was to (re)describe a system of government, and form “a more perfect Union” after the prior Articles of Confederation had proved unsatisfactory. It was not to write a criminal code. The states were then (and still are) the primary forum for criminal law.

    It has been revealed that so the Constitution defines only one crime, treason (in Article III, section 3). It mentions a few others, like “Bribery” (in Article II, section 4) and “Breach of the Peace” with a general reference to “Felony” (in Article I, section 6). And of course the Impeachment Clause (Article II section 4) mentions “high Crimes and Misdemeanors,” without definition. Again, states were expected to take care of the substantive definition and application of virtually all criminal law. (However, as I explained some years ago, the First Congress in 1790 did enact over two dozen federal crimes.).

    Yet a large focus of the Bill of Rights is criminal procedure.

    It has been revealed that three years after the Constitution was drafted, the Bill of Rights focused on criminal law rights in at least four proposed amendments (the Fourth, Fifth, Sixth, and Eighth). I won’t list the multitude of rights captured there, but they form the bulk of all criminal procedure law school classes today. The right to be free from unreasonable governmental searches and compelled self-incrimination, and the rights to counsel, jury trials, and no cruel and unusual punishments – and much more – are all embodied in the Bill of Rights.

    One example from last term: in Villareal v. Texas, the court had to interpret the Sixth Amendment right to “Assistance of Counsel” to decide (unanimously) that a criminal trial judge can order that the defendant not discuss their ongoing testimony with their attorney during an overnight recess.

    Sources indicate that why was the Bill of Rights so focused on criminal procedure rights? It’s a fun question to ask students, or at the Thanksgiving table if things get slow. Sooner or later someone gives the soundbite answer: “because most of the constitution’s framers were crooks.” They were certainly guilty of treason – then and still today a capital (that is, death penalty) offense, as well as other crimes (violence, destruction of property, incitement, and more). Had the revolutionary Framers been captured by the government (the British) they likely would have been hung. Instead, during the course of the revolution, numbers had been tried in absentia, found guilty by officials (not juries), and had their houses searched and occupied by troops. Cruel and unusual torture had been inflicted on some captured compatriots. When constitutional ratifying conventions demanded a bill of rights, protections from unfair criminal processes were therefore topmost on the minds of many drafters (if not perhaps “the People” at the time).

    Sources indicate that (Another aside: ask your lawyer friends to compare the content of civil procedure versus criminal procedure classes today. The latter full-semester course is almost entirely constitutional law – I used to call my own crim pro class “Con Law Three.” By contrast, civil procedure classes, also a full semester, focus largely on the nitty-gritty details of federal rules, only occasionally wandering into statutes or the Constitution.).

    In addition to the four explicitly criminal-focused amendments, you might then add general constitutional ideas that are bound to capture some criminal law cases: the First, Second, Third, and Ninth Amendments. The First Amendment’s direction, that “Congress shall make no law” regarding (“respecting”) or abridging freedoms of religion, speech, and the press, is a constitutional law command against criminal laws as well as civil. So too is a protection of a right to keep and bear arms, and to not have government troops quartered in “any” house (not just your own).

    And then consider the “great generalities” of the Constitution.

    In his 1921 Storrs Lectures at Yale Law School (subsequently published as “The Nature of the Judicial Process”), future Supreme Court Justice (and then Newly introduced York Court of Appeals Judge) Benjamin Cardozo discussed “the great generalities of the Constitution.” Among these, the Equal Protection and Due Process Clauses of the 14th Amendment are huge sources of criminal law doctrine. Just last term, for example, the procedural steps required to apply the Equal Protection Clause against racial (and other) bias in jury selection, and the idea that due process and judicial integrity requires a “miscarriage of justice” exception to guilty plea waivers, received focused Supreme Court attention (in Pitchford v. Cain and Hunter v. United States, respectively).

    Sources indicate that criminal law cases focused on the meaning and application of these broad constitutional requirements arise regularly almost every Supreme Court term. Indeed, as I advise my students every year (again I aspire to teach with a smile, not didactic cynicism): no matter what arguments you make on the defense side of a criminal case, always add the words “and in violation of due process” to preserve at least a thread of a constitutional argument that you may not even perceive at the moment.

    It has been revealed that in addition to equal protection and due process, I (and others) would add the Ninth Amendment, which speaks of unspecified “rights … retained by the people.” Justices have sometimes suggested that the Ninth and Tenth Amendments state nothing but “truism[s],” while other Supreme Court decisions have relied (at least in part) on the Ninth. For some, invocation of the Ninth Amendment may provoke if not laughter (it having been referred to by one academic as a “constitutional jester”), then a distinctly conservative or “originalist” rejection. Yet other conservative scholars such as John Yoo and Calvin Massey (my late former colleague) have written expansively about it. As Randy Barnett has argued, the Ninth Amendment “means what it notes,” and is “a significant guarantee of individual liberty.” If that is so, then it is (or could be) another source of criminal law protection for criminal defendants.

    For example, Griswold v. Connecticut recognized a constitutional right to privacy in the criminal law context, resting in part (and almost entirely for three justices) on the Ninth Amendment. Less controversially, perhaps, Chief Justice Warren Burger later invoked the amendment in the 1980 case of Richmond Newspapers v. Virginia to support an “unarticulated” constitutional right for the public (and the press) to attend criminal trials. And in 2000, even Justice Antonin Scalia agreed (in a solo dissent to Troxel v. Granville, a non-criminal case) that the Ninth Amendment recognizes unenumerated rights. When you tell your Thanksgiving dinner companions that criminal law is constitutional law, don’t forget the Ninth Amendment.

    So criminal law is, very often, constitutional law.

    Sources indicate that thus it should be unsurprising (as detailed in my Annual Review of the Supreme Court’s Term, Criminal Law booklet) that 22 of the court’s merits decisions last term that address criminal law involved elements of constitutional law (17 fully argued cases plus five summary (unargued) decisions). That’s a substantial percentage of the court’s entire merits opinions docket, roughly a quarter or more.

    Statutory criminal law cases also often involve constitutional law.

    By now I hope that you are persuaded: criminal law is (often) constitutional law. “But wait – there’s more!” When you combine the Constitution’s Supremacy Clause with the oft-cited judicial doctrine of constitutional avoidance, criminal cases requiring statutory interpretation also fall into this category. That is, these are criminal law cases that involve consideration of constitutional law. Advocates in statutory cases often raise potential constitutional objections to a criminal statute or to its application in their case, or they may raise constitutional law ideas in favor of their preferred interpretation. In addition, an understanding of constitutional doctrine can be necessary to properly evaluate the merits of a statutory claim. The bottom line is that, in many statutory criminal cases, explication or consideration of constitutional law is necessary or helpful to explain the result.

    Industry observers note that just a few examples from last term: In Barrett v. United States, the court had to mine the details of double jeopardy doctrine to agree, unanimously, that a statute could be interpreted as not permitting two convictions for a single act, thereby avoiding a constitutional problem. In Olivier v. City of Brandon, the court had to examine Olivier’s constitutional claims in order to decide whether the federal civil rights statutes were a proper vehicle for him to sue under. And in Whitton v. Dixon, the court had to briefly explain the constitutional Giglio doctrine, regarding a prosecutor’s failure to disclose exculpatory impeachment information, to reverse an application of the federal habeas corpus statue.

    Immigration cases also often require constitutional law, either to dispose of the merits or to resolve statutory issues in them. Last term’s birthright citizenship case, Trump v. Barbara, is the most obvious example. Because immigration and criminal law cases are often intertwined – consider recent ICE arrests, detentions, and criminal violation grounds for removal – I include them in my annual review as well as the purview of this column. And even civil cases that I consider related to criminal law often require consideration of constitutional law concepts. For example, last term’s Hencely v. Fluor Corp., rejecting a claim of government contractor immunity, required consideration of constitutional preemption doctrine.

    In other words, criminal law mixed with constitutional law is everywhere.

    Last week, many of us were focused on the details of elections around the country, big and small. And next week, after Thanksgiving, will be chock full of criminal law and related Supreme Court oral arguments. So I’ve tried to give you a break today, and provide a few thoughts that are, perhaps, entertaining, or provocative, or at least interesting ways to navigate your mealtime gatherings (rather than focusing on the usual subjects). For some of you, perhaps this column has simply demonstrated what you already considered obvious; or perhaps it has opened interesting linkages in your mind between constitutional law and criminal law. In any case, thanks for reading this far. Next week I hope you are fortunate enough to breathe relaxing breaths, give thanks, and dwell not on legal minutiae but on what really matters.

    Rory Little has been teaching Constitutional and Criminal Law topics at UC Law SF (formerly Hastings) for over 30 years, after 12 years of practice.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A Texas law firm is apologizing for an ad in Maxim magazine that created such an outcry among truckers that truck stops pulled the publication from their shelves.

    According to recent reports, the full-page ad for San Antonio law firm Villarreal & Begum demonstrated a picture of a truck cab beneath the words “serial killer.” Both the law firm and Maxim are apologizing for the ad after Pilot Flying J and TravelCenters of America pulled the magazine from their shelves. Publications with stories include HDT Trucking Info, TheTrucker.com, CSPNet.com, KIROTV.com and LandLinemag.com.

    The copy read: “3,561 people died on America’s highways last year. Another 2.36 million were injured. You need a law firm you can Trust. You need Experience. You need Strength. You need Villarreal & Begum. We’re proven leaders in prosecuting cases involving death and catastrophic injury.”.

    In a recent development, in its statement, the law firm notes it never intended “to disparage the hardworking Americans that drive tractor-trailers for a living. Our intent was to reach out to those individuals who have been involved in catastrophic accidents as a result of irresponsible drivers. The ad was inartfully created, and we could see how it may have caused our message to be misconstrued. We recognize the service that truck drivers provide to this nation and acknowledge that most truck drivers are safe and responsible drivers.”.

    Maxim also issued a statement saying the ad “does not reflect the beliefs or opinions of the people at this magazine, which recently has begun operating under latest ownership.” The ad has been pulled from Maxim’s digital copy and replaced with facts about the trucking industry.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    South Africa is mourning the death of Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka, a trailblazing political leader who served as the country's first woman deputy president and later held a senior United Nations post.

    JOHANNESBURG (AP) â Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka, South Africa’s first female deputy president and a United Nations under-secretary-general, has died at age 71, the South African government announced Friday.

    Meet the researcher tracking hallucinations in legal filings

    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Damien Charlotin grew up as a self-proclaimed geek in Brittany, France, playing video games and learning to code.
    • Those coding skills came in handy when as a doctoral student at the University of Cambridge in 2020, Charlotin built a database with nearly 200,000 legal citations to accompany his thesis on citing authorities in international legal disputes.
    • Charlotin still remembers introducing his students to OpenAI two days before the generative artificial intelligence company released ChatGPT in 2022.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    November 23, 2026, 10:11 am CST.

    Damien Charlotin grew up as a self-proclaimed geek in Brittany, France, playing video games and learning to code.

    Those coding skills came in handy when as a doctoral student at the University of Cambridge in 2020, Charlotin built a database with nearly 200,000 legal citations to accompany his thesis on citing authorities in international legal disputes. That led to teaching legal data analysis—essentially coding for lawyers, he says—at HEC Paris and Sciences Po Paris.

    Charlotin still remembers introducing his students to OpenAI two days before the generative artificial intelligence company released ChatGPT in 2022.

    Recent findings suggest that “They had no idea what was coming,” Charlotin states. “And obviously, you can never have again that kind of awe on their faces.”.

    Industry observers note that charlotin transitioned easily into teaching about AI and the legal profession. In April 2025, he was discussing the limits of large language models in the legal domain when he realized there wasn’t much data about hallucinations. He decided to pull together information into what became the AI Hallucinations Cases database, which tracks legal decisions in cases where generative AI produced fake citations and other hallucinated content.

    Sources indicate that “I’m very empirically minded, and I wanted to be sure that hallucinations were actually an concern,” Charlotin claims. “And if so, to what extent?”.

    Recent findings suggest that with the help of referrals, targeted searches and automated extraction and tagging, Charlotin has identified 2,334 cases that cite hallucinated material. His coverage of the United States is particularly strong because court information is more accessible, he claims, but he also highlights cases from dozens of other countries.

    According to recent reports, and his conclusion? Hallucinations, while often highlighted, are not a major problem.

    “I don’t think there are that many cases, all things considered,” Charlotin says.

    Charlotin’s AI Hallucinations Cases database has been shared by media around the world.

    “For the first six months, I had something like four or five interviews a week,” Charlotin states. “It was kind of weird, to be honest. That’s easier now, but still, there is a lot of interest.”.

    According to recent reports, A latest trend in Charlotin’s data is now catching the legal profession’s attention. Court filings that contain hallucinations seem to be decreasing this year, from 462 in the first quarter to 435 in the second quarter. He logged 376 cases in the third quarter, and so far, only 117 in the fourth quarter.

    Charlotin largely attributes the decline in hallucination cases to improved AI models and tools.

    “Hallucinations are mostly a technical matter, and you can to some extent fix them by making sure citations are checked by something else, which is something the legal tech side is doing more, or making sure citations of anything are limited to things the model knows particularly well,” Charlotin notes.

    Other factors may contribute to a decrease in fake AI citations, including that lawyers who misused AI already have been identified and disciplined in many situations, Charlotin adds.

    While Charlotin hopes that legal practitioners will continue to use his database to track trends with hallucinations or to keep an eye on relevant cases in their jurisdictions, he also says it is the impetus for other important areas of his work.

    In a recent development, he spends a lot of time researching and writing, both as part of his ongoing legal scholarship on AI and the law, and for Artificial Authority, his Substack publication that covers developments in these areas. Charlotin has focused recently on adversarial inputs, which he describes as “attempts to fool or manipulate the AI-mediated legal work on the other side for one’s own purposes.”.

    It has been revealed that “The basic idea is that if you know the other side is using AI and delegating everything to AI, you will be incentivized to exploit it, and you can exploit it,” claims Charlotin, who serves as a AI strategy consultant to law firms. “I think that will become even more common.”.

    Based on his database, Charlotin also created Pelaikan, an automated legal citation and reference verification tool for legal professionals. It has web, desktop and Word versions, and he is now developing Claude and ChatGPT integrations.

    While not his main gig, Charlotin has a few clients and is happy to help them shave time off their workdays, he says.

    Charlotin is bringing his experience with AI and the law to this side of the pond.

    In a recent development, as a co-director of the AI-Enabled Lawyer Lab at the University of California College of the Law, San Francisco, Charlotin is designing and teaching an introductory course on legal AI tools. Currently in the pilot phase, it will roll out to the entire cohort of nearly 400 2L students next year, he notes.

    In the course, Charlotin aims to teach law students how AI models actually work; how to use any platform, no matter the vendor; and how to rely on their own judgment even when incorporating AI into their workflows.

    “The main logic throughout the course is that the use of AI by law students, and in fact by anyone, should be as far away from the notion that AI is a magic button as possible,” Charlotin indicates.

    According to recent reports, charlotin, who is married and has a 1-year-old daughter, will mostly teach virtually but plans to travel to San Francisco a few times each semester. He’ll also be in the city in early December to teach practicing lawyers and legal professionals about AI during an intensive three-day program.

    “I’m very busy, maybe I should focus on one thing,” jokes Charlotin, who along with everything else, practices in public international law and international arbitration.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, gemini is a global crypto and Web3 platform founded by Cameron and Tyler Winklevoss in 2014, offering a wide range of simple, reliable, and secure crypto products and services to individuals and institutions in over 70 countries. Our mission is to unlock the next era of financial, creative, and personal freedom by providing trusted access to the decentralized future. We envision a world where crypto reshapes the global financial system, internet, and money to create greater choice, independence, and opportunity for all — bridging traditional finance with the emerging cryptoeconomy in a way that is more open, fair, and secure. As a publicly traded manufacturer, Gemini is poised to accelerate this vision with greater scale, reach, and impact.

    The Role: Senior Software Engineer (Mobile).

    As a Senior Mobile Engineer on the Predictions team, you'll own the mobile experience for Gemini's CFTC-regulated prediction markets exchange. You'll build and ship trading interfaces for event contracts — from order entry and position management to real-time market data — within Gemini's React Native app. You'll work closely with product, design, backend, and compliance to bring latest contract types (binary, range, combo) to market on mobile and drive activation and retention for a fast-growing product line.

    Salary Range: The base salary range for this role is between $140,000 - $200,000 in the State of Upcoming York, the State of California and the State of Washington. This range is not inclusive of our discretionary bonus or equity package. When determining a candidate’s compensation, we consider a number of factors including skillset, experience, job scope, and current market data.

    Industry observers note that in the United States, we offer a hybrid work approach at our hub offices, balancing the benefits of in-person collaboration with the flexibility of remote work.     #146983. The Supreme Court and profanity

    The Supreme Court and profanity

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2215 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, around 2 p.m.
    • The station later stated it had chosen Carlin’s routine because it was an “incisive satirical view of the subject under discussion,” in the style of other great satirists like Mark Twain or Mort Sahl.
    • Recent findings suggest that before playing the routine, the host had warned that it included language some listeners might find offensive and suggested they return in 15 minutes if they were inclined toward offense.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, around 2 p.m. on October 30, 1973, John Douglas was driving with his 15-year-old son when he heard a litany of profanity come over the radio. Upcoming York’s WBAI, a nonprofit radio station, was airing a program on modern attitudes toward language. Near the end, the station played George Carlin’s “Filthy Words” routine, which begins with the comedian saying he’d been thinking about “the words you couldn’t say on the public airwaves; the ones you definitely wouldn’t say, ever.” He went on to repeat those words several times, contrasting them with words like “bastards,” “hell,” and “damn,” which were mostly acceptable, and showing how even some of his list of seven were perfectly fine in other contexts. His point was to show the absurdity of profanity.

    The station later stated it had chosen Carlin’s routine because it was an “incisive satirical view of the subject under discussion,” in the style of other great satirists like Mark Twain or Mort Sahl. Carlin, the station explained, was doing more than “mouthing obscenities.” He was “using words to satirize as harmless and essentially silly our attitudes towards those words.”.

    Recent findings suggest that before playing the routine, the host had warned that it included language some listeners might find offensive and suggested they return in 15 minutes if they were inclined toward offense. But about a month later, John Douglas complained to the Federal Communications Commission about the transmission which he mentioned was “garbage” and had been broadcast in the presence of his “young son.” He was the only listener to do so. A member of Morality in Media who frequently listened to the station to “see how far” they’d go, Douglas later acknowledged that he had laughed out loud at the bit but “did not appreciate WBIA’s ‘smart-alecky’ on-air provocations.”.

    The previous year, Carlin had been arrested after performing an earlier version of the same routine, but a judge threw out the charge. This time, the FCC found the broadcast “indecent,” and put its order in the station’s license file.

    That order ended up before the Supreme Court.

    Early in its order, the FCC acknowledged that Congress had forbade it from censoring broadcasts. But Congress had also prohibited the broadcast of “obscene, indecent, or profane” language, and the Commission thought Carlin’s broadcast fit the bill. In the FCC’s view, the ban on “indecent” language covered not just obscenity, but also patently offensive language when there was a reasonable risk of children listening. Late at night, when children were unlikely to be listening, the same material might be okay if it appeared in a work of serious literary, artistic, political, or scientific value.

    Two commissioners thought even that was too permissive. Charlotte Reid believed “this language to be totally inappropriate for broadcast at anytime” and thought the commission’s standard did “not go far enough.” Commissioner James Quello took much the same view. “Garbage is garbage,” he wrote, whether children were listening or not.

    The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, however, set aside the order in a 2-1 vote, with one judge believing it violated the statutory ban on censorship and the other saying it violated the First Amendment. The FCC appealed to the Supreme Court.

    At oral argument, which was held in April of 1978, several justices made their distaste for Carlin’s bit plain. When Pacifica’s lawyer stressed that the station had warned listeners beforehand and aired the monologue as part of an educational program about language, Chief Justice Warren Burger incredulously asked, “This is educational in your view?” And when counsel defended the material’s artistic value, Justice Thurgood Marshall responded, “Well, I’m not an expert, but if that’s artistic, deliver me.” Justice William Rehnquist, for his part, tested the limits of Pacifica’s position with a hypothetical involving a single four-letter word repeated for an hour. Would the FCC be powerless to prohibit that? Justice John Paul Stevens, however, seemed troubled by the potential reach of the FCC’s position, given that the prohibition on indecency could be enforced through criminal law.

    One striking exchange concerned the Justice Department’s position to argue separately, and more narrowly, than the FCC. The solicitor general’s office urged that the First Amendment prevented the government from barring particular words outright for a substantial part of the day without regard to context, even if the FCC could constitutionally regulate “indecency” to some extent. Rehnquist sharply asked why the Justice Department was arguing against the FCC, what interest it had in seeking a narrow construction of an act of Congress, and whether the solicitor general, as the government’s lawyer, could ever argue that an act of Congress was unconstitutional.

    Recent findings suggest that justice Lewis Powell also pressed the DOJ on the reasons behind its departure from the FCC, noting that the DOJ had supported the FCC in the court below. “That is true, and that is an embarrassment to us,” Deputy Solicitor General Louis Claiborne acknowledged, suggesting it was because the matter had been handled there by the Antitrust Division rather than the Criminal Division. Another explanation, which he did not mention, was that the administration had changed.

    Industry observers note that the court ultimately ruled 5-4 that the FCC could constitutionally treat this broadcast as “indecent” under the governing statute, and that the government could constitutionally prohibit indecency even though it fell short of legal obscenity. Stevens wrote for Burger, Justice Harry Blackmun, Powell, and Rehnquist, having apparently struggled with the case and flip-flopped before settling against Pacifica. The Commission had treated the piece as a nuisance, and, as the court had observed in Village of Euclid v. Ambler Realty Co., a nuisance could be as simple as “a pig in the parlor instead of the barnyard.” He concluded that “when the Commission finds that a pig has entered the parlor, the exercise of its regulatory power does not depend on proof that the pig is obscene.” Though the holding expanded the government’s power to regulate speech, Stevens emphasized broadcasting’s pervasive presence in the home and its accessibility to children, the fact the piece was broadcast during the daytime, and the narrowness of the holding. He did not address late night broadcasts or the “occasional expletive.”.

    Stevens had only three votes for some parts of his opinion. Powell, joined by Blackmun, wrote separately to object to Stevens’ suggestion that the level of protection that speech receives should depend on a judge’s perception of that speech’s value. For them, the combination of repeated, patently offensive language, an afternoon broadcast, and children’s ready access was enough to resolve the case. Powell also addressed the concern that the decision could end up “reduc[ing] the adult population . . . to [hearing] only what is fit for children”: adults could buy tapes or hear the same words at theaters.

    Sources indicate that justice Potter Stewart dissented, joined by Justices William Brennan, Byron White, and Marshall. Stewart would have resolved the case on statutory grounds. He read “indecent” to reach only obscene material, and everyone agreed that Carlin’s monologue fell outside that category. His opinion recalled his concurrence in Jacobellis v. Ohio, where he voted to overturn an obscenity conviction for showing a French film with an explicit love scene. Stewart understood obscenity narrowly, but declined to define it, famously observing in that case, “I know it when I see it, and the motion picture involved in this case is not that.”.

    According to recent reports, brennan wrote a separate dissent, joined by Marshall, that went further. He agreed with Stewart on the statute and noted he would ordinarily refrain from addressing the constitutional question, but he found “the Court’s misapplication of fundamental First Amendment principles so patent, and its attempt to impose its notions of propriety on the whole of the American people so misguided,” that he was “unable to remain silent.”.

    Brennan disputed the analogy between a radio broadcast and an intrusion into the home. Listeners voluntarily turn on the radio, and they can voluntarily turn it off. In perhaps his sharpest passage, he wrote:.

    In a recent development, brennan also questioned the majority’s reliance on protecting children. He read the court’s precedents as allowing the government to shield children from material that was obscene as to them. In his view, Carlin’s routine fell outside that category. Keeping it off the radio during the afternoon cut off access for adults as well as children. And while the majority had invoked parents’ right to raise their children as they saw fit, Brennan thought the FCC had somewhat ironically made the choice for them.

    Recent findings suggest that finally, he remained unconvinced that the court’s reasoning would reach only cases like Carlin’s. Among the things it could sweep in were “literary works, novels, poems, and plays by the likes of Shakespeare, Joyce, Hemingway, Ben Jonson, Henry Fielding, Robert Burns, and Chaucer,” “a good deal of political speech, such as the Nixon tapes,” and even portions of the Bible. In his view, the public, and not the court, should have the power to weed out “worthless and offensive” speech in a marketplace “unsullied by the censor’s hand.”.

    According to recent reports, brennan and Marshall had joined together in another Supreme Court opinion involving the F-word. In Cohen v. California, they joined Justice John Harlan II’s opinion protecting the right to wear a jacket emblazoned with “Fuck the Draft.” Stewart joined it too (not surprisingly, Burger and Blackmun dissented). Brennan brought Cohen straight into his Pacifica dissent; as he made clear, changing the words can change what the speaker communicates, something that applies especially well to Carlin because the taboo words were themselves the subject of the routine. And Brennan thought telling listeners to buy a record or pay to see Carlin live missed what it meant to hear the routine on the radio.

    In a recent development, in closing, Brennan wrote that the majority had only “confirm[ed] Carlin’s prescience as a social commentator.” (It was interesting that Marshall, who sounded distinctly unimpressed by the claim of artistic merit at oral argument, joined him, perhaps especially here.) As Brennan pointed out, Carlin had made fun of the rules about which words you could say on the air, and the court had exemplified the very attitude he was satirizing. To top it all off: Appended to the opinion is the transcript of Carlin’s routine, giving his “indecent” words a permanent home in the U.S. Reports.

    At the 2002 Billboard Music Awards on Fox, Cher dispatched the critics who’d spent decades predicting her downfall with “So f*** ’em.” At the 2003 awards, Nicole Richie asked whether anyone had tried getting cow manure out of a Prada purse, then used the F-word to describe how hard it was. The next year, after Bono called U2’s Golden Globe win “really, really f***ing brilliant,” the FCC confirmed that even a single expletive could be indecent, and it later applied that approach to the two earlier Fox broadcasts.

    Recent findings suggest that in 2009, the Supreme Court took up the dispute in FCC v. Fox Television Stations. Writing for a 5-4 majority, Justice Antonin Scalia held that the FCC had adequately explained its change in policy under the Administrative Procedure Act, leaving the First Amendment question open. Justice Clarence Thomas joined the majority but wrote separately to question Pacifica’s holding. On remand, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 2nd Circuit struck down the policy as unconstitutionally vague.

    The case returned to the Supreme Court in 2012 and all eight participating justices agreed on the result (Justice Sonia Sotomayor recused herself). Justice Anthony Kennedy’s opinion held that the FCC had failed to give Fox fair notice that fleeting expletives could trigger an indecency finding, but once again left both Pacifica and the First Amendment question open. Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg wrote separately to say that Pacifica was wrong from the start and deserved reconsideration. But while the court has had several cases involving curse words since, it has yet to take up the question directly.

    It has been revealed that in 2004, the FCC dismissed complaints related to the airing of Saving Private Ryan on the basis that the film’s curse words helped convey the soldiers’ experience. But just two years later, it slapped a station with $15,000 in fines for airing a Martin Scorsese documentary about Blues music that contained profanity. In 2020, the FCC received over 1,300 complaints about Jennifer Lopez and Shakira’s halftime show, though it never took any action against the network. And in February 2026, FCC requested transcripts of Bad Bunny’s Superbowl halftime performance before ultimately finding no violation.

    Half a century after Carlin’s seven dirty words, the FCC’s continued and seemingly arbitrary application of its indecency laws demonstrates the prescience of Brennan’s dissent and the need to finally answer the question of whether the Constitution prohibits the “dominant culture” from trying to force “groups who do not share its mores to conform to its way of acting, thinking, and speaking.”.

    Anastasia Boden is a Senior Attorney at the Pacific Legal Foundation, where she brings civil rights lawsuits that advance the Constitution’s promises of equality and economic opportunity.

    Safrudin stated that the six suspects were being investigated under multiple provisions of Indonesiaâs Criminal Code related to treason, conspiracy and preparation to overthrow the government. The offenses carry penalties ranging from long prison terms to life imprisonment or death.

    He mentioned the suspects are alleged to have committed criminal acts by ordering, participating in or encouraging others to carry out treason âwith the intention of depriving the president of his liberty, rendering the president unable to govern and/or overthrowing the government.â.

    Investigators have also linked some of the suspects to large anti-government demonstrations held across Indonesia in recent months and confiscated 20 One Piece flags, featuring imagery from the popular Japanese anime and manga franchise that has recently been adopted by some Indonesian anti-government protesters as a symbol of resistance, as well as 735 million rupiah ($45,000) in cash.

    When asked whether the protests were connected to the case, Safrudin remarked that some of the suspects had been involved in organizing or supporting certain activities that are now under investigation.

    Safrudin noted that investigators were continuing to investigate whether the suspects had supported or influenced other political movements aimed at weakening the government.

    âWe are tracing what activities they supported, what activities they may have exploited and other related matters,â he noted.

    Police had seized 39 electronic devices as evidence, including cellphones, laptop computers, central processing units and hard drives, Safrudin remarked.

    Authorities also confiscated hundreds of black T-shirts that investigators said were connected to the case, including 250 shirts bearing an image of a firearm and the slogan âAll Cops Are Bastardsâ and 251 shirts featuring the phrases âAware of being extorted, aware of being burned, aware of being impoverished,â alongside a three-finger salute and the hashtags #IndonesiaSadar or #AwareIndonesia.

    It has been revealed that police didn’t immediately provide evidence supporting the treason allegations or explain how the seized items were linked to the alleged conspiracy. It wasn’t immediately clear whether the suspects had obtained legal representation. There was also no immediate public response from Listyo Sigit or the other suspects.

    The announcement marks a dramatic escalation of the wiretapping scandal that has already led to the dismissal of several senior police officers and prompted parliamentary scrutiny of Indonesiaâs law enforcement and intelligence institutions.

    Authorities remarked that the investigation remains ongoing and that additional suspects could still be identified.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, in September, Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson received an award named after the late Justice William Brennan, a liberal lion.
    • Industry observers note that since joining the court in the summer of 2022, Jackson has sought to promote her understanding of that view.
    • Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

    According to recent reports, in September, Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson received an award named after the late Justice William Brennan, a liberal lion. In her acceptance speech, Jackson discussed Brennan’s role as the Supreme Court became more conservative, noting that he “believed that even his dissents could make a difference and remind the nation that the pursuit of equal justice under law is an ongoing effort.” Jackson indicated that she agreed with that idea, telling the audience that she saw “dissent[s] as more than just a disagreement with the outcome of a case, I see them as an expression of faith in the future and a demonstration of hope.” As she put it, “However desolate the moment feels, we who write for a future age have hope that the noble and collective work of bending the long arc of the law toward justice will continue.”.

    Industry observers note that since joining the court in the summer of 2022, Jackson has sought to promote her understanding of that view. Although she has been consistently part of the court’s liberal bloc, even among the three Democratic appointees she has forged a unique role. As her invocation of Brennan suggests, it often appears that her goal is not simply to express disagreement with the majority, but to offer an alternative vision and to speak to the public directly – even if she does so without the support of her fellow liberals.

    Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

    The Second Amendment and an "unusually dangerous" approach to dicta

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1833 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Please note that SCOTUS Outside Opinions constitute the views of outside contributors and do not reflect the opinions of SCOTUSblog or its staff.
    • In a recent development, on November 10, The Fresh York Times published an article suggesting that a major piece of the Supreme Court’s Second Amendment jurisprudence is premised on a misquote by the late Justice Antonin Scalia in his 2008 majority opinion in D.C v.
    • According to the Times piece, “[t]he consequences of Justice Scalia’s use of ‘and’ rather than ‘or’ have been profound”: “Since all guns are dangerous, courts have had to focus instead on determining whether a type of firearm is unusual, often parsing marketing data and consumer surveys to gauge a weapon’s popularity.” Presumably, if Scalia had used the phrase “dangerous or unusual,” it would be easier for legislatures to ban even certain commonly owned firearms because dangerousness alone would be sufficient to bring a category of weapons outside the amendment’s protective sphere.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Please note that SCOTUS Outside Opinions constitute the views of outside contributors and do not reflect the opinions of SCOTUSblog or its staff.

    In a recent development, on November 10, The Fresh York Times published an article suggesting that a major piece of the Supreme Court’s Second Amendment jurisprudence is premised on a misquote by the late Justice Antonin Scalia in his 2008 majority opinion in D.C v. Heller, in which the court held that there was an individual right to possess firearms. The essence of the piece is that Scalia used the phrase “dangerous and unusual” to describe those weapons not protected by the right to keep and bear arms, attributing this terminology primarily (or perhaps solely) to the 18th century British jurist William Blackstone. Yet Blackstone’s writings instead use the phrase “dangerous or unusual.”.

    According to the Times piece, “[t]he consequences of Justice Scalia’s use of ‘and’ rather than ‘or’ have been profound”: “Since all guns are dangerous, courts have had to focus instead on determining whether a type of firearm is unusual, often parsing marketing data and consumer surveys to gauge a weapon’s popularity.” Presumably, if Scalia had used the phrase “dangerous or unusual,” it would be easier for legislatures to ban even certain commonly owned firearms because dangerousness alone would be sufficient to bring a category of weapons outside the amendment’s protective sphere.

    It has been revealed that the Times story has reverberated quickly, with strong backlash from conservative lawyers and scholars. Such disagreements have focused largely on the specific citation Scalia used. Law professor Jonathan Adler, for example, has argued that the citation to Blackstone was one among many, and additional sources that Scalia cited used the “and” formulation. Others have responded that Scalia was anything but sloppy, which would be especially true when it came to such an influential and important source.

    Sources indicate that both sides, though, seem to be burying the lede. In my view, this is a story not about historical errors or the nuances of legal citation. Rather, it is about how judicial dicta that was never intended to lay down broad, permanent rules has taken on a life of its own, and how other justices on the Supreme Court subsequently canonized Scalia’s stray language by turning it into a “test” that would govern any number of future cases – when it’s not at all clear Scalia ever contemplated this or would have endorsed any such thing.

    As most law students and lawyers are well aware, the holding-dicta distinction is deeply rooted in American jurisprudence: generally speaking, the holding is the analysis necessary to resolve the actual case before the court, and everything else in an opinion is dicta (this comes from the Latin phrase “obiter dictum,” or “mentioned in passing”). Fundamental to that distinction is that dicta, while it may be persuasive, is not precedential. As Chief Justice John Marshall wrote in 1821, the reason for not deferring blindly to dicta is “obvious”:.

    The late Judge Richard Posner once similarly emphasized the risk that dicta “can be misleading if carelessly lifted from the case-specific contexts in which they were originally uttered … That is why courts in assessing the binding effect of previous decisions distinguish between the dicta, which are the inessential parts of the opinion, and the holding.” Circuits vary in their approach to Supreme Court dicta, generally deferring more heavily to such language when they find it thoroughly considered or supported, but the court is, of course, never bound by its own dicta.

    Recent findings suggest that in fact, Scalia himself was no fan of relying heavily on dicta from prior Supreme Court decisions. In a 1993 opinion, he criticized a group of dissenting justices by noting that their position found “support, if at all, only in the dicta of this Court’s opinions.” This was, in Scalia’s view, as good as no support at all. Indeed, Scalia rejected reliance on “drive-by … rulings” not fully considered by the issuing court, even if not purely dicta. In his 2015 decision for the court in Kerry v. Din, Scalia excoriated a proposition advanced in a dissenting opinion as resting solely on “dictum in a footnote” and then observed that “[t]he footnoted dictum that Justice Breyer proposes to elevate to constitutional law is a dangerous doctrine.” He further joined opinions that rejected prior dicta as unprincipled, especially when greater investigation revealed reasons for caution.

    Scalia’s position was nuanced – for example, he once joined a dissent by Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg that endorsed reliance on certain dictum as persuasive – yet a cautious approach to dicta is consistent with his broader judicial philosophy as well. He was at times willing to jettison even precedential decisions squarely applicable to the case at hand when those decisions were contrary to original public meaning. Unconsidered dicta, presumably, would then be far lower in the pecking order.

    It has been revealed that returning to Heller and the phrase at glitch, it’s hard to argue that the “dangerous and unusual” passage from Heller is anything but dicta. The issue in Heller was whether a Washington, D.C. ordinance “generally prohibit[ing] the possession of handguns” violated the Second Amendment, or if there was an individual right to keep arms for one’s self-defense. Scalia’s majority opinion answered in the affirmative, as “the American people have considered the handgun to be the quintessential self-defense weapon.” D.C. never argued that handguns were entirely exempt from protection because they were especially dangerous. The question of dangerous and/or unusual weapons was not at issue in the case; accordingly, it wasn’t thoroughly investigated through the adversarial process.

    Sources indicate that rather, after canvassing the historical evidence and concluding it supported an individual-rights view of the Second Amendment, Scalia turned to the nature of the right he had just explicated. In three short paragraphs not necessary to the holding, he explained why the amendment did not authorize gun keeping-and-carrying by anyone in any circumstance; rather history revealed limitations on the right, such as “the carrying of ‘dangerous and unusual weapons.’”.

    Whatever the purpose of this section – Justice John Paul Stevens later suggested the language was proposed by Justice Anthony Kennedy (the crucial fifth vote in Heller) in exchange for joining the majority – it was far from necessary to resolve the case at hand.

    Recent findings suggest that so how did such dicta become relevant? In the 2016 case Caetano v. Massachusetts, decided after Scalia had passed away, the justices unanimously overturned a Massachusetts Supreme Court decision upholding that state’s ban on stun guns in a criminal prosecution of a woman who used this weapon to defend herself from an abusive ex-boyfriend. Justice Samuel Alito issued a concurring opinion (joined by Justice Clarence Thomas) that performed an interesting maneuver. Seizing on the fact that the per curiam opinion in that case referenced Scalia’s “dangerous and unusual” formulation, Alito turned Scalia’s language into a doctrinal test: “As the per curiam opinion recognizes, this is a conjunctive test: A weapon may not be banned unless it is both dangerous and unusual.” But the per curiam had done no such thing; rather, that opinion simply cited the passage in Heller as referring to one limitation on the right to keep and bear arms. And the per curiam said that the lower court in that case had faltered by concluding that any weapon not in common use in 1791 was per se unusual, not by failing to use a conjunctive test.

    (Ironically, Alito has his own well-publicized objections to giving past Supreme Court dicta undue veneration – his opinion for the court in Dobbs heavily suggested that Roe’s viability framework was entitled to less weight in the stare decisis analysis because it was initially mere dicta, “the Court’s own brainchild [for which n]either party advocated.”).

    From there, the “dangerous and unusual” language took on a life of its own. In 2022’s New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen, in which the court struck down New York’s concealed-carry law, the majority set forth a test for Second Amendment constitutionality privileging historical evidence above all else. At the first step of that test, a court determines whether the conduct at issue is protected by the right to keep and bear arms, which is where the exclusion of dangerous and/or unusual weapons becomes relevant. If the banned weapon is not protected by the Second Amendment (for, say, being “dangerous and unusual”), a constitutional challenge is dead on arrival. If, on the other hand, the plaintiff can show the weapons are protected, then the burden switches to the government to provide historical evidence to support its regulation. (The consequences may be even greater, as some have argued that “usualness” (or “common use”) conclusively establishes not only threshold protection for the weapon but also that any legislative ban is ahistorical and thus unconstitutional.).

    Sources indicate that this test has divided the judiciary in recent years. For example, a Massachusetts federal judge evaluating a challenge to that state’s AR-15 ban recognized the apparent disconnect between Heller and Blackstone but nevertheless noted that “the Supreme Court has expressly stated . . .that the relevant tradition is one of regulating ‘dangerous and unusual weapons.’” The Massachusetts judge found these weapons were not in “common use,” and, in any event, a historical tradition of responding to technological advances by regulating specific weapons supported the ban. By contrast, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit interpreted Scalia’s language to signal that widespread ownership of AR-15s and large-capacity magazines meant any legislative attempt to ban them was unconstitutional. The “dangerous and unusual” framework has led other judges on a search for ownership statistics and sales data to assess a weapon’s popularity, triggering sharp debate over whether a test that ultimately turns on commonality is even workable.

    According to recent reports, this is particularly relevant since the court is currently preparing to hear oral argument in Viramontes v. Cook County, a Second Amendment challenge to state and local bans on AR-15s, on December 2. While the recent attention to Scalia’s citation may trigger discussion at oral argument, most justices are now likely to treat “dangerous and unusual” as an established standard and ownership statistics as definitive proof that AR-15s are not unusual and thus protected. Absent from this, however, will be the fact that this standard did not emerge from any well-reasoned, litigation-tested analysis making it deserve deference in the first place – especially under Scalia’s own approach to judging.

    The debate over Scalia’s Blackstone citation, then, has obscured a more notable problem: the Supreme Court’s decision to treat its past dicta as doctrine that can settle the outcome of cases on which the court has never passed.

    Andrew Willinger is an Assistant Professor at Georgia State University College of Law, where he teaches constitutional law and civil procedure.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Kit is the email marketing platform experts choose to grow their audience, deepen their relationships, and build a business around the work they love. For coaches, YouTubers, authors, podcasters, and other creatives, there isn't a better marketing hub to rely on to grow audiences, automate email marketing, and sell digital products — all within one platform.More importantly, there isn't a team more committed to helping creators earn a living. We're on a mission to help creators earn $1 billion using our creator marketing platform. We have always been 100% independent and 100% remote.We are proud to have built a product that our customers love, and we look for people who have enthusiasm and belief in our mission, vision, and values to join our team. We're also embracing AI thoughtfully — both in how we build and how we hire to ensure our team is adaptable, innovative, and ready for what's next.

    We’re looking for a senior product designer to be the first dedicated designer on our product growth team, shaping how creators get set up, see value in their first days, and enjoy a seamless upgrade experience. Kit ships fast, and the product growth team builds the frameworks and systems that connect creators to the value in their plan as the product keeps changing. We need a designer who can balance rapid experimentation with long-term value for our creators.

    Sources indicate that product growth is a upcoming team at Kit, formed earlier this year. In the six months since, we’ve found our rhythm and started to move the numbers, but we’re still shaping how we work, how we prioritise and where we focus in the long term. As the team’s designer, you’ll be the design voice for growth, with real influence over how the team works and what it builds.

    Recent findings suggest that you'll own the design of the moments that move our funnel: onboarding, activation, free trials, upgrade and upsell flows, pricing and checkout, and billing. You'll work in a team that learns by shipping, through A/B tests and ship-and-measure changes, and you'll use data to decide what to try next.

    This is a full-time IC role for a designer who loves connecting design decisions to numbers, moves promptly without sacrificing quality, and is excited about using AI to accelerate outcomes.

    We need someone who thinks deeply about user behaviour, interaction design and the product experience, and who is proactive about finding the next opportunity rather than waiting for a spec.

    You'll report to Dan Winer, Director of Product Design, and join a small, high-impact product design team right now consisting of four senior product designers and a senior design engineer. From day one, you’ll be part of the product growth team’s product trio alongside the product manager and engineering manager, shaping the team’s vision, priorities and how we work. You’ll also work closely with the team’s engineers.

    First week: Get to know Kit’s product and the product growth team’s goals. Get access to Figma, Linear, Mixpanel and our other reporting tools. Take part in get-to-know-you calls with the team.

    First month: Get up to speed on how we track and measure creator behaviour in Mixpanel, Omni and Clarity, which experiments are running now, and what we’ve learnt from past ones. Join the product trio’s planning and prioritisation discussions, and ship a small experiment or two, with support from the Director of Product Design as you take ownership of the growth work.

    It has been revealed that first six months: Own design across the team’s work, which spans growth (onboarding, activation, trials and upgrades) and billing (checkout, plan changes, downgrades and cancellation). This might include personalising onboarding, improving free-to-paid conversion or simplifying our payment flows. By six months, the team should rely on you for a clear picture of how creators move through these flows, where they get stuck and why. You’ll help the team run more and better experiments, from forming a hypothesis to reading the results. We don’t have dedicated researchers, so you’ll talk to creators, run usability tests, track the impact of your work and proactively suggest iterations.

    Recent findings suggest that first year: Help the team improve our activation, free-to-paid, trial conversion, and early retention rates, so that more creators upgrade, stay on Kit, and find real value. Turn our upsell, discount and plan change moments into one coherent experience instead of a set of one-off prompts.

    Interaction design for complex web applications, with a strong eye for visual hierarchy and detail.

    Grounding design decisions in the creator’s voice through interviews, usability testing and customer feedback, partnering with the PM so it shapes what we build as well as how.

    Designing flows that change depending on who’s seeing them, like free, trial and paid accounts, or creators upgrading and downgrading.

    Designing onboarding, activation, upgrade, pricing, checkout or billing flows.

    Experiment design and reading results, including knowing when an A/B test is the right approach or when to just ship and track.

    Defining what events to track so the team can measure what you shipped, using tools like Mixpanel.

    Clear written and visual communication of design rationale, including async walkthroughs.

    Around 5+ years as a product designer on SaaS or other complex web-based products.

    Led design on growth, monetisation or onboarding work and can point to its impact on metrics, ideally including retention or quality of conversion, not just volume.

    Worked in a cross-functional team with a product manager and engineers, shipping continuously.

    Worked within and contributed to an established design system.

    A portfolio that reveals how research or data informed your decisions and what happened as a result.

    Bonus: designed pricing, billing or initiative change experiences.

    Curious about why customers behave the way they do, and about what the numbers aren’t telling you.

    Comfortable being wrong in public and sharing what you don’t know, not just what you do.

    Proactive and self-directed, with a bias for shipping.

    Excited about AI and pragmatic about how to use it.

    Low ego and comfortable giving and receiving direct feedback.

    Preferring to execute designs handed down from a product manager.

    Treating a conversion win as the finish line, without checking whether those creators stay with Kit and find value.

    Wanting long, highly-refined projects with little contact with data or results.

    Discomfort with experiments that fail or with changing direction based on what we learn.

    Focusing on visual polish without deeper thinking about user behaviour and business outcomes.

    Being philosophically opposed to using AI in your work.

    Needing well-established processes and a fully defined roadmap from day one.

    We're 100% remote with team members across the globe. We work mostly on East Coast time - so if you're based on the West Coast of the United States, Europe, or Asia, you might have a few early mornings or late evenings. We do our best to keep things reasonable, but a little time zone juggling comes with the territory.

    Kit has standardized salaries based on position, no matter where you live. For this role, we're hiring at level 4 ($172,000). Level is determined based on experience and our interview process.

    It has been revealed that we cover up to $2,280 per month toward medical premiums, with dental and vision premiums fully covered. We offer Health Insurance plans through Aetna.

    Industry observers note that $2,000 equipment allowance for your first two years, $1,000 budget every following two years. Organization-provided laptops are issued to every Kit team member and are not included in the equipment budget.

    Individual learning + development budget ($3,500/year).

    Creator meetup budget ($50/month) to connect with creators over coffee, lunch, or other in-person meetups.

    Childcare benefit up to $3,000 annually through JOON.

    Twenty (20) days of paid time off during each year of employment.

    Up to six weeks of paid bereavement leave, medical leave, and disaster after six months of employment, two weeks of each paid leave in your first six months.

    Fantastic in-person or virtual retreats with the team twice a year.

    #146970. Latest Update: As Netflix and Disney sniff around, YouTube hypes its creators’ “world-class, studio-quality” programming at L.A. Premieres event

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2463 w)
