    Latest Update: Netflix is rallying post-Warner Bros. with revised IRL installation intends and a potential bid for NBCUniversal

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (603 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tubefilter

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • OK, so Netflix failed to buy Warner Bros.
    • That potential acquisition is apparently top of wishlist for Netflix (and Variety already deemed it “Hollywood’s Next Significant Deal”), but Comcast co-CEOs Mike Cavanagh and Brian Roberts say they’re not selling.
    • Recent findings suggest that well, according to Bloomberg, the current strategy is for Netflix to revamp its approach to permanent interactive IRL installations, aka Netflix Houses.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    OK, so Netflix failed to buy Warner Bros. Discovery.

    What if it bought NBCUniversal, tho?

    That potential acquisition is apparently top of wishlist for Netflix (and Variety already deemed it “Hollywood’s Next Significant Deal”), but Comcast co-CEOs Mike Cavanagh and Brian Roberts say they’re not selling.

    Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

    Recent findings suggest that well, according to Bloomberg, the current strategy is for Netflix to revamp its approach to permanent interactive IRL installations, aka Netflix Houses. The streamer first unveiled these in 2023, with a demo setup that looked like someone stocked the gift shop in Jurassic Park with merch of the laser murder doll from Squid Game.

    At the time, Josh Simon, Netflix’s then-VP of Consumer Products (now CEO of collectibles tech giant Funko) said the concept for Netflix Houses came from knowing “fans love to immerse themselves in the world of our movies and TV shows,” and “thinking a lot about how we take that to the next level.”.

    Netflix had flirted with pop-ups before that; those were mainly focused on selling stuff. Make no mistake, Netflix Houses are also focused on selling stuff, but in a Disney World kind of way, where fans pay $39 to enter the House and head through an art gallery-esque space filled with themed exhibits like exclusive theater indicates, movie/TV set recreations, VR experiences, and arcade games. There are cafeterias and merch shops, but by and large the things to buy share billing with things to do.

    The Houses are permanent installations (for now just in Dallas and Philly, with one planned to open in Vegas in 2027) but the exhibits within rotate regularly to keep up with whatever’s trending on Netflix.

    This year, for example, the Houses were renovated to feature animated smash megahit KPop Demon Hunters. They’ve also spotlighted Stranger Things, One Piece, Wednesday, and the aforementioned Squid Game.

    Recent findings suggest that per Bloomberg, Netflix initially planned to open dozens of Houses across the U.S., focusing on quieter suburban areas away from downtowns. It wanted to snap up spaces in malls, which are not doing very well and might be willing to rent for cheap.

    But apparently the results from its first two Houses haven’t been quite what Neflix expected, so it’s pausing openings beyond Vegas until it can reassess.

    It has been revealed that people familiar with the matter told Bloomberg the Philadelphia location has daytime draws like mini golf and a movie theater, but doesn’t see much traffic at night. Dallas, meanwhile, is breaking even financially, and has done well with larger groups and corporate events.

    Netflix is also planning to see what comes from its Las Vegas location. Vegas, as you may know, is not in fact a quieter suburban locale–so if the House there proves to be profitable, with more traffic than Dallas and Philly, Netflix could reconsider where it opens in the future.

    People familiar with the matter said Netflix is also looking at maybe taking Houses overseas. But wherever the next one ends up, it probably won’t open for at least another year, they said, until significant data from all three flagship U.S. locations is in.

    Now, with all this in mind, it’s worth remembering Netflix just shock-fired its longtime Chief Content Officer Bela Bajaria and replaced her with Peter Rice, Disney‘s former General Entertainment Chairman. Film chief Dan Lin is out too. Clearly, Netflix hopes to revamp more than its IRL installations…and perhaps it’s hoping Rice’s Disney EXP comes in handy with the Houses?

    TikTok’s next microdrama is an 81-episode musical series from Barlow & Bear

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Four and a half years after winning a Grammy for The Unofficial Bridgerton Musical, the songwriting duo known as Barlow & Bear has something new in store for TikTok viewers.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Four and a half years after winning a Grammy for The Unofficial Bridgerton Musical, the songwriting duo known as Barlow & Bear has something new in store for TikTok viewers.

    Sources indicate that abigail Barlow and Emily Bear are two of the creators behind To Die For Love, an 81-episode musical microdrama co-produced by TikTok and Ampersand. According to TikTok, the series follows “an ambitious half-witch vying for her coven’s crown. When she falls for a mortal, their romance takes an unexpected turn, forcing an impossible choice between family and the love of her life.”.

    Barlow & Bear created an original score for To Die For Love, while Barlow co-wrote the script alongside Oscar-nominated writer/director, actor, and opera singer Julia Aks.

    Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

    Barlow also stars in the series opposite Broadway vet Derek Klena. Executive producers include Ampersand CEO Agnes Chu, Benj Pasek, Justin Paul, Danielle Perelman, Chris Crema, Matthew Ko, and Kevin Weaver.

    “Making To Die For Love has been one of the most rewarding creative experiences of our careers,” Barlow and Bear said. “We love a pressure cooker, and building an entire musical in under five months proved that meaningful storytelling isn’t about time—it’s about the story and the people bringing it to life.”.

    This isn’t the first creator-driven microdrama TikTok has brought to life. Earlier this year, Issa Rae’s media company, HOORAE, struck a deal with the platform to produce short-form web series for both TikTok and its companion app PineDrama. The first vertical series to emerge from that partnership, Screen Time, had racked up over 620 million views on TikTok and PineDrama as of late October, making it both platforms’ most-viewed show to date.

    TikTok doubled down on that success last month when it declared a new microseries-focused partnership with Made By Us Studios, which describes itself as a “first-of-its-kind, Hollywood-grade studio designed for the creator economy and powered by creator management tech giant MADE BY ALL.”.

    It has been revealed that now, TikTok is forging ahead into the world of musical microdramas. To Die For Love will be available exclusively on TikTok and PineDrama, with all 81 episodes premiering December 21. The original soundtrack will be released by Atlantic Records.

    #146916. Industry News: Marketers will spend $116B on creators in 2026. They’re “cannibalizing” other budgets to do it.

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (490 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tubefilter ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Marketers will spend $116B on creators in 2026. They’re “cannibalizing” other budgets to do it.

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (490 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Tubefilter

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Marketers are investing more money into the creator economy—and reallocating their existing advertising budgets to pay for it.
    • According to a recent report from strategic advisory, consulting, and research firm Madison and Wall, marketer spend on creators is set to grow “+15% in 2026 to $116 billion globally, up from $101 billion in 2025.”.
    • Based on that trajectory, the report predicts that the advertiser-funded creator economy will hit $178 billion by 2030.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Marketers are investing more money into the creator economy—and reallocating their existing advertising budgets to pay for it.

    According to a recent report from strategic advisory, consulting, and research firm Madison and Wall, marketer spend on creators is set to grow “+15% in 2026 to $116 billion globally, up from $101 billion in 2025.”.

    Based on that trajectory, the report predicts that the advertiser-funded creator economy will hit $178 billion by 2030.

    Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

    Recent findings suggest that madison and Wall compiled its study by isolating marketing funds dedicated to “creator related activity” (i.e., “spending deployed to creators, agencies, platforms, technology vendors, and media networks to achieve marketing, commerce, or brand objectives”). Other forms of creator income—such as subscriptions, merch, and platform payouts—weren’t taken into account.

    The report further separated creator marketing spend into five distinct categories: audience-led spend, media-led spend, asset-led spend, infrastructure-led spend, and miscellaneous.

    Of those categories, Madison and Wall found that media-led spending—aka “the paid amplification of creator content”—accounts for the largest piece of the pie at 44% (or $52 billion) of 2026 spend.

    It has been revealed that audience-led spending (“the traditional sponsored-post and ambassador model”) ranks second at 28%, while asset-led spending (“where brands pay for content rather than reach”) accounts for 12% of the market. Infrastructure-led spending (net revenue kept by agencies, managers, and platforms) and miscellaneous (events, gifting, licensing, etc.) bring up the rear at 8% and 7% respectively.

    According to recent reports, on a global scale, Madison and Wall found that the U.S. was responsible for 43% of creator spending in 2025, well above its ~35% share of global advertising. The closest runners-up were the UK (which accounts for 5% of global creator spending) and Germany (4%).

    One of the key takeaways of Madison and Wall’s report concerned the origin of marketing funds dedicated to creator advertising.

    Recent findings suggest that the firm noted that “creator growth is largely funded by reallocation rather than newly introduced money. Interviews with stakeholders across the ecosystem point to three sources: traditional media, notably TV; digital performance media, including paid social, programmatic and search; and creative production budgets. Because creators draw on several existing budget pools at once, the creator economy can keep outgrowing advertising without marketers creating new budgets.”.

    One senior operations executive told Madison and Wall that “80% of the time we are cannibalizing another budget, whether it’s TV or [something else].”.

    Overall, the firm found that creator spending grew at an 18% compound annual growth rate (CAGR) between 2020 and 2025, as compared with 12% for advertising.

    It has been revealed that that gap doesn’t seem likely to close anytime soon. According to the firm’s projections, creator spending is set to grow ~12% a year through 2030—putting it well ahead of the 6% growth expected for the advertising economy.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • YouTube has come under fire in the past for how it handles content posted by people suspected of heinous crimes, but its policy has remained the same: It will only terminate a channel if someone is convicted in a court of law, and if their YouTube content is directly related to their crime.
    • Now, the platform has refused a request from the Prison Service of England and Wales to remove content from Russell Brand‘s channel.
    • The comedian and actor will be in prison for over a decade after being convicted of three counts of sexual assault and one count of rape, stemming attacks on four different women.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    YouTube has come under fire in the past for how it handles content posted by people suspected of heinous crimes, but its policy has remained the same: It will only terminate a channel if someone is convicted in a court of law, and if their YouTube content is directly related to their crime.

    Now, the platform has refused a request from the Prison Service of England and Wales to remove content from Russell Brand‘s channel.

    The comedian and actor will be in prison for over a decade after being convicted of three counts of sexual assault and one count of rape, stemming attacks on four different women. Presiding British High Court judge Mr Justice Bennathan described Brand as a “sexual predator” whose behavior demonstrated a “series of lies” and “staggering arrogance.”.

    Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

    In the upload, Brand asserts innocence, telling viewers, “As you know, I am not guilty for the offences I have been jailed for, so something strange is happening.”.

    Authorities contacted YouTube via “an established mechanism the prison service has with tech companies to request deletion of material,” per the BBC, to ask that Brand’s video be removed.

    But YouTube isn’t willing to scrub it–at least not yet.

    “We are aware of the fresh content and our teams are investigating,” a spokesperson from YouTube parent Google told the BBC. “We suspended Russell Brand’s channel from the YouTube Partner Program in September 2023. The channel has not been able to monetize on YouTube since then.”.

    Recent findings suggest that that’s a pretty typical order of operations for YouTube. In past cases with creators like Adnan Ahmed, Austin Jones, and Ian Rylett, YouTube suspended monetization on their channels when allegations surfaced and the legal process began, and then terminated their channels once convictions were filed.

    He also holds Christianity-themed “Sunday services” with Gallacher.

    The assaults Brand was convicted for all happened before 2009; he made his YouTube channel in 2007, but didn’t start uploading videos until 2012. YouTube could potentially claim they’re not related based on timeline alone, since Brand–who was already a celebrity outside of YouTube–didn’t use his channel or digital clout to connect with his victims.

    So the question here is: Does YouTube amend its policies to ban convicted criminals–or specifically convicted sex offenders–from posting on its platform? What if their newly introduced content is directly related to their crimes, as Brand’s is?

    United Kingdom Prime Minister Andy Burnham got involved after YouTube’s initial denial, telling the platform (and other socmed platforms) to “show some decency and take these videos down.”.

    “[It’s] time that we focus on the victims and think about them,” he added, instead of “hearing from a convicted criminal.”.

    In a recent development, “I would call on those social media companies to take these interviews down,” Burnham added. “Why are we having to hear from him? We shouldn’t be, and certainly [victims] shouldn’t be hearing from him.”.

    The attention on YouTube’s refusal has sparked a bit of a Streisand effect. Commenters are flocking to Brand’s video, sneering at Burnham, the U.K. government, and activists for their attempts to remove it.

    “Had no intention to watch until the government told me not to,” one top-liked comment says.

    “If the government tells you not to watch a video, you really need to watch that video to find out why,” another claims.

    Other socmed platforms have cut Brand off. Instagram, Facebook, and WhatsApp–all owned by Meta–have culled his accounts, thanks to policies that prohobit convicted sex offenders from owning and/or operating accounts.

    YouTube bows out of World Cup rights race; Netflix might step up

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (376 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Tubefilter

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • YouTube was an official “Preferred Platform” for the 2026 FIFA World Cup, and it worked to make the partnership a high scorer.
    • It also exercised the broadcast rights that came along with being a Preferred Platform: By the time Spain took it all home, YouTube’s World Cup content had drawn nearly 2 billion unique viewers, 550 million of whom tuned in from their TV sets and bumped YouTube’s Nielsen numbers.
    • But that success apparently isn’t enough of a carrot for YouTube to go bigger and bid for TV rights to future World Cups.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    YouTube was an official “Preferred Platform” for the 2026 FIFA World Cup, and it worked to make the partnership a high scorer. It tapped creators to film promo content, then brought them pitchside to film dozens of videos at the tournament’s top matches around the world.

    It also exercised the broadcast rights that came along with being a Preferred Platform: By the time Spain took it all home, YouTube’s World Cup content had drawn nearly 2 billion unique viewers, 550 million of whom tuned in from their TV sets and bumped YouTube’s Nielsen numbers.

    But that success apparently isn’t enough of a carrot for YouTube to go bigger and bid for TV rights to future World Cups.

    Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

    According to Atlantic sports columnist Andrew Marchand, YouTube declined to submit a bid for American broadcast rights to the 2030 and 2034 World Cups.

    There were rumors that YouTube planned to go out for rights, but a source familiar with the matter confirmed to Marchand that YouTube is not tossing its hat in the ring.

    It’s not alone: Apple, ESPN, NBC, and the newly formed Skydance have also declined to bid. Between their various subsidiaries, that knocks out chances of the World Cups airing on CBS, TNT Sports, Paramount+, HBO Max, and Telemundo.

    According to recent reports, so who does want the rights? Marchand reports Fox–which had the rights for 2026–is going out for them. But, perhaps surprisingly, the other top frontrunner seems to be Netflix.

    Or maybe it’s not so surprising–Netflix already has rights to the 2027 Women’s World Cup, and we know it’s willing to pay major for exclusive sporting events, so maybe the men’s Cup is exactly the complement it’s looking for.

    We don’t know what the winner will end up paying here, but Fox paid $485 million to air the 2026 tourney in the U.S. Netflix did say it expects to close out the year spending money on developing original content and investing in sports (and now it has freer cash considering its failed bid to buy Warner Bros. Discovery). The World Cup just might be one of those investments.

    YouTubers IShowSpeed, Michelle Khare, MrBeast, Dhar Mann, Spaceskits, Jordan Howlett, Kylie Kelce, and fern all took home prizes from the inaugural Clio Creator Awards.

    An offshoot of the long-running Clio Awards, which debuted in 1959 to honor excellence in advertising around the world, the Clio Creator Awards are presented by YouTube and backed by Influential, the content creator-led marketing firm Publicis Groupe bought for $500 million in 2024.

    The first Clio Creator event brought host Terry Crews to the Dolby Theater in Los Angeles to hand out awards in categories like Creator & Brand Collaborations, Public Relations, Integrated Campaign, and Written Content.

    Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

    According to recent reports, “Creators aren’t just participating in culture, they’re shaping it,” Nicole Purcell, CEO of the Clios, mentioned in a statement. “The inaugural Clio Creator Awards recognize the incredible talent and originality driving this industry forward, from creators building their own communities to brands finding new ways to connect with audiences. These are storytellers whose influence extends far beyond their platforms, and we’re proud to give them the recognition they deserve.”.

    “As the presenting sponsor of the awards and home to the creators shaping culture today, YouTube is proud to champion the craft and expertise that goes into creator partnerships and creator-led work,” YouTube remarked in a firm blog post.

    Industry observers note that “A huge congratulations to every creator, brand, and agency honored last night. Spanning across Shorts, live streams, podcast and cinematic content for the biggest screens, these winners show that creators on YouTube are taking their content and brand partnerships to new heights,” it added.

    Creator x brand collabs have gotten nods in other ad industry events and award shows (including Tubefilter’s own Streamy Awards)–but the fact that a legacy show like the Clios are embracing the creator world, and that these awards are backed by a Publicis Groupe subsidiary, points to further enmeshing of our space with traditional entertainment.

    • Industry observers note that topper Guild is getting into the animation game.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Each week, we handpick a selection of stories to give you a snapshot of trends, updates, business moves, and more from around the creator industry.

    This week, GTA VI is making billions, a heartwarming viral moment is becoming a Lifetime movie, and TikTok wants you to know it’s a massive deal in the music biz.

    Industry observers note that topper Guild is getting into the animation game. Content creator Topper Guild is teaming up with animation company Toonstar to create an original series, which is set to premiere on YouTube. “Animation is a medium I’ve always wanted to work in, but I didn’t think it was possible to maintain that same pace my fans expect, or retain the creative control I have with my live-action content,” Guild stated. “But Toonstar changed that. They’re unlocking animation for the creator economy.”.

    Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

    Kane Parsons is going from Backrooms to BAFTA. YouTuber-turned-filmmaker Kane Parsons has been named as one of 14 creatives participating in BAFTA North America’s 2026 Breakthrough US cohort. The Backrooms director will join the program alongside rising entertainment icons like Heated Rivalry’s Connor Storrie and The ‘Burbs creator Celeste Hughey.

    Entrepreneurs On Fire has been acquired. John Lee Dumas has reportedly agreed to sell the company behind his business podcast, Entrepreneurs On Fire, to PR firm Pathos Communications for $3 million in cash, plus up to $6 million in “performance payments.” Dumas will continue to host the show as part of a three-year deal.

    Recent findings suggest that youTube could pay billions over child safety concerns. Sources familiar with the matter reportedly told Bloomberg that YouTube is preparing to settle a wave of lawsuits regarding its allegedly “addictive” design by paying roughly $3 billion to thousands of school districts.

    TikTok dropped some significant stats in its 2026 Music Impact Report. According to a study commissioned by TikTok from Luminate, 94% of songs that entered the Billboard Global 200 last year went viral on TikTok first—a ten-percentage-point jump from 2024. The report also noted that songs “that go viral on TikTok spend four times longer on the Billboard Global 200 than those without a viral moment.”.

    A Meta vet is coming to OnlyFans. Whitney Rosenthal is coming aboard as OnlyFans’ first global head of creator partnerships. The exec previously worked at Meta and YouTube; most recently, she served as vice president of global creator podcast platforms at Podimo.

    Streaming platforms are going all in on creator content. Newly introduced data from Ampere Analysis reveals that U.S. streaming services debuted over 3,700 hours of “creator-led programming” in Q3 2026, up from 1,934 in the previous quarter. Distribution of new creator-led content on SVOD services also rose 75% over the last quarter, with Amazon Prime Video alone contributing over 230 hours (per Net Influencer).

    GTA VI made billions on day one. Rockstar Games announced Friday that Grand Theft Auto VI hit $3.79 billion during its first day of retail sales, “setting a new record for entertainment across any medium, and becoming the biggest entertainment launch in history.”.

    It has been revealed that A microdrama studio will produce content for Black audiences. NBCUniversal and HarbourView Equity Partners are throwing their financial weight behind June, a microdrama studio launched by Will and Dom Packer. The studio will focus on the development, production, and acquisition of original vertical dramas aimed at Black viewers.

    Freeman & Forrest has a newly introduced majority owner. Falfurrias Management Partners has made a majority investment in B2B influencer marketing firm Freeman & Forrest. Co-founder Emily Freeman will stay on board as CEO, while co-founder Forrest Brazeal will continue in his role as president.

    e.l.f. set a world record at TwitchCon. e.l.f. Cosmetics made history at TwitchCon 2026 by breaking the Guinness World Record for most people applying make-up simultaneously. The beauty brand’s massive GRWM included 733 in-person participants—and that was only the start of e.l.f.’s onsite activations at the con.

    Sources indicate that lifetime is turning a viral friendship into a film. In 2016, Wanda Dench and Jamal Hinton spread holiday cheer across the internet by sharing the heartwarming story of how an accidental text turned into an invitation to Thanksgiving dinner. Ten years later, Dench and Hinton have turned their shared Thanksgivings into an annual tradition—and now, Lifetime is turning it into a movie.

    Industry observers note that the Denver Broncos are tapping into the power of anime. The anime horse girls of Umamusume: Pretty Derby have become a familiar sight for sports fans in recent months, with appearances at events ranging from Grand Prix de Paris to Japan’s Super GT championship. Now—as part of an official collaboration with the Denver Broncos—two of the anime’s most recognizable characters will be on hand to support the team at Empower Field when they face the Miami Dolphins next month.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Asmongold & co. might be major mad that Grand Theft Auto VI‘s story hinges on being good to your über-hot girlfriend, but everyone else is diggin’ it.

    It has been revealed that the long-long-awaited Rockstar title that’s turning out to be “a bug zapper for chuds” is officially the single biggest video game ever made. It cleared $3.8 billion in sales on day one, and has the second-highest critics’ consensus rating of all time, outdone only by Nintendo‘s 1998 masterpiece The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time (which just got a nice remake that released nearly in tandem with GTA VI).

    Of course, all this hype has translated into enormous traffic for digital video platforms and the creators who stock them.

    Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

    Twitch also saw a 33% bump in the number of channels going live: It peaked at almost ~200,000 concurrent live channels, with GTA VI making up 127,400 of them.

    YouTube Gaming, meanwhile, drew 33.2 million watch hours, and Kick generated 48.4 million.

    Now, to be clear, these are not GTA VI-specific numbers. These are across entire platforms. But it’s a good look at things holistically, because as GTA VI rose, other titles’ traffic seeped toward it.

    According to recent reports, on Twitch, GTA VI streams generated 76.81 million watch hours in the first 48 after its release. And though it didn’t include numbers, Streams Charts reports that “[h]undreds of creators also set personal audience records as fans tuned in to watch their first steps in Rockstar’s latest release.”.

    Nearly every other top title fell in watch hours, including World of Warcraft (down 31%), League of Legends (down 7%), Dota 2 (down 12%), Counter-Strike (31%), and Fortnite (39%).

    The only game that didn’t lose traction was Escape from Tarkov, which went up 11%; this is due to developer Battlestate Games holding a Twitch Drops giveaway during this timeframe, where streamers are required to broadcast Tarkov gameplay, and viewers are incentivized to tune in because they’ll get exclusive in-game items.

    In a recent development, the game that saw one of the biggest traffic drops was, perhaps unsurprisingly, Grand Theft Auto V, whose viewership plummeted 49%. (More on that in a minute.).

    Over on Kick, Streams Charts spotted an interesting data point: While Just Chatting streams had a 19% drop on Twitch during the first 48 hours, Kick’s Just Sleeping category jumped 176% thanks to streamers holding 24/7 GTA VI marathon streams where they left things running while they caught catnaps.

    In a recent development, things got muddy on YouTube. Streams Charts reports that many streamers went live under the GTA V category instead of GTA VI, “making it virtually impossible to separate interest in the older game from traffic driven by the new release.”.

    Industry observers note that streams Charts tracked YouTube watch time falls in top games like Fortnite (60%) and Mobile Legends: Bang Bang (30.4%), while Apex Legends and Free Fire rose 70% and 59%, respectively. Like with Tarkov‘s Twitch traffic, Apex and Free Fire‘s boosts were thanks to view-generating events. In Apex‘s case, it was invitational tournament FFL APEX BLOCK PARTY, and for Free Fire, it was the FFWS Global Finals 2026 competition.

    In two days, GTA VI‘s total watch hours (counted across Twitch, YouTube, Kick, and eight other platforms) beat all other game debuts’ first-week numbers.

    The closest to catching it is Valorant, which dropped in April 2020 and generated 150.48 million watch hours in its first seven days. Then there’s Elden Ring, which dropped February 2022 to 79.08M hours, and Diablo IV in June 2023 to 74.34M hours. Hogwarts Legacy, Cyberpunk 2077, and Resident Evil Requiem are all down in the 40-60M hours range.

    Now, this does not mean any game will lose traffic long-term, aside from potentially GTA V. Here’s why: GTA VI is the shiny newly introduced thing on the block. Once streamers churn through its story, most will go back to their usual niches. The ones who stick around post-campaign will be playing GTA VI Online, and those are the folks that were probably still streaming GTA V when VI came out.

    In a recent development, GTA has one of the biggest roleplaying communities of any game, and VI provides an expansive new playground for folks who are into that. Everyone else will enjoy the campaign and the viewership bump it brings, then head back to Apex or WoW or League of Legends.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    Vox users can watch videos and listen to podcasts in the app, but reading stories requires a paid subscription.

    Vox has rolled out its first mobile application, the publication best known for its explanatory journalism announced Wednesday morning.

    Growing membership is a “key priority,” managing editor for audience and membership Bill Carey noted. Vox believes launching the app is one way to do that. A Vox membership costs $5 per month, or $60 per year, and offers ad-free versions of podcasts and unlimited access to all of the website’s contents.

    Sources indicate that RELATED ARTICLEVox is revamping its editorial strategy to redefine what ‘Voxxy’ meansHanaa' TameezNovember 8, 2021Strengthening its relationship to its audience is only becoming more crucial for Vox. The app launch comes at a time when news publishers are increasingly trying to keep users on their own platforms amid growing preferences for AI summaries, news creators, and industry-wide traffic declines.

    It has been revealed that “The move toward developing our membership program in the last couple of years has really been about understanding how notable it is for us to build more community and to foster that loyalty [of our] audience,” Carey said. “When we were looking at that, it really felt like an app was a good way to continue pointing in that direction.”.

    Vox isn’t the only news outlet focusing on mobile apps. The Verge — Vox’s former sister publication under Vox Media — named traffic declines as one of the reasons why it aims to launch its own app next year. The Wall Street Journal’s head of digital, Taneth Evans, recently said that the Journal makes its app more useful to consumers by offering all of its mediums in one place. Evans also said that news publishers “need to give people reasons to open an app beyond simply offering news.”.

    “Websites will become a service for agents,” Evans remarked. “Apps are gonna be the thing that humans will connect with.”.

    Recent findings suggest that vox declined to provide website traffic numbers, but data from Comscore shows that the website’s unique visitors decreased by 36% year-over-year between September 2025 (7.4 million) and September 2026 (4.8 million). Archived data from SimilarWeb shows the site had 20.8 million visits in September 2021.

    “Vox isn’t immune to the larger trends that have led to web traffic declines in recent years, but those only represent a portion of our audience,” Carey said in an email. “Vox is focused on building audience engagement across platforms, with social video views up 86% year-over-year and newsletter audience up 14%.”.

    Industry observers note that “Even if there wasn’t a decline in search traffic, as everyone has been seeing — and we still get members from search — we want to create that relationship with our audience,” publisher and editor-in-chief Swati Sharma noted. “People know Vox and they have a relationship with Vox. We have a younger audience that’s on all of these different platforms. I think it is definitely a part of building that relationship ourselves.”.

    Recent findings suggest that that the app makes all Vox content accessible in one place for current and future members also signals the “un-siloing” of the newsroom overall, Sharma stated. Vox presently has 78 editorial employees.

    RELATED ARTICLESwati Sharma is leading a new era in Vox’s mission to “explain the world”Hanaa' TameezMay 6, 2021When Sharma, who has helmed Vox.com since 2021, first arrived, she found that Vox’s main mediums (text, audio, and video) “weren’t in service of one another.” The “silos” allowed teams to build their own audiences and products. But while teams discussed story ideas with each other and during editorial meetings, “they all [needed] to go into their creative spaces and find what works for their medium and not be in service of just one larger section.”.

    It has been revealed that that’s changed over the past five years, Sharma said. Each team — text, video, and audio — does a little bit of everything now. Text reporters appear on podcasts and in videos, while podcasters and hosts also write their own newsletters.

    “In a lot of newsrooms, there’s one dominant form, and at Vox, there wasn’t. They’re all really important,” Sharma said. “[Senior correspondent] Dylan Scott is on our Unexplainable podcast talking about Alzheimer’s. [Host and editorial director] Astead Herndon does a newsletter and a Substack Live every week, and he does a podcast. That’s the future for us, and that’s where our whole newsroom is moving, where those silos are done and you can basically do everything.”.

    Meta pledges to consult publishers before finalizing its newly introduced terms

    📅 28 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (933 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Niemanlab

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing.
    • Sources indicate that we have sent a confirmation link to .
    • Meta will complete “a full consultation” with news industry leaders before implementing its controversial latest terms — even if it means another delay, an executive for the social media company revealed today.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    Sources indicate that we have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    Meta will complete “a full consultation” with news industry leaders before implementing its controversial latest terms — even if it means another delay, an executive for the social media company revealed today.

    “We’ve heard publishers’ feedback on our proposed ads and business terms revision. We care deeply about our partners and do not blueprint to make policy changes without a full consultation with industry groups and leaders,” vice president of communications Andy Stone tweeted. “We’re committed to getting this right, and as we expect this consultation could extend beyond November 20, in which case we’d delay implementation of the updated terms. Until then our existing terms remain in place.”.

    Meta did not answer Nieman Lab’s questions about which news industry groups and leaders Meta plans to consult.

    Industry observers note that the proposed terms have drawn criticism because they would permit broad scraping of websites “associated with” business accounts, and potentially allow Meta to use that scraped content to train its AI models, with no option to opt out. Last week, Meta unveiled it would push back implementation of its new terms to November 20 in order to “explain to our partners and stakeholders what’s changing and what’s not — including how Meta uses web crawlers and the fact that content owners will still be able to use robots.txt to signal preferences,” a Meta spokesperson told Nieman Lab. Meta had previously revised its new terms to remove the word “train.” No version of the terms has included language about respecting robots.txt preferences.

    Shortly after Stone’s announcement, a Norwegian court blocked Meta’s terms from taking effect on November 20 until the court had assessed their legality, the country’s public broadcaster NRK reported.

    Sources indicate that “We are satisfied that the court has agreed with us that Meta holds a dominant position in the relevant market and that the new terms are unreasonable,” remarked Lene Eltvik Vindfeld, MBL’s board chair, in a news release. “We are also pleased that the court recognizes that the alternative is that media companies risk losing control over editorial content built up over many years.”.

    It has been revealed that since Nieman Lab first reported on the terms on October 15, publishers and politicians around the world have pushed back, filing complaints with national competition authorities, calling on the European Commission to investigate, and writing letters to Meta’s CEO Mark Zuckerberg. Two United States senators — California Democrat Adam Schiff and Tennessee Republican Marsha Blackburn — each separately wrote to Zuckerberg, insisting that the company withdraw the terms as they’re at the moment written.

    “After I raised serious concerns about Meta’s intends to scrape and abuse creators’ content, I am pleased the tech giant is finally acknowledging the concerns of publishers and content creators,” Blackburn said in a statement to Nieman Lab on Wednesday. “While this is a step in the right direction, a vague promise to consult with industry stakeholders and potentially delay implementation is not nearly enough. Meta must commit to meaningful changes that protect the intellectual property rights of American creators, and I will continue holding the company accountable until it does.”.

    According to recent reports, on October 21, the European Publishers Council signed onto a joint letter to the European Commission, asking the Commission to block the terms from taking effect. The letter claims that Meta’s terms violate the Digital Markets Act, a law passed in 2020 to curb the dominance of substantial tech companies and create fairer competition across the region.

    EPC executive director Angela Mills Wade said on Wednesday that the organization has not heard from Meta about its letter or its concerns.

    Sources indicate that “We welcome Meta’s offer to consult publishers fully, and to delay implementation if necessary,” Mills Wade said in an email to Nieman Lab. “However, that consultation must lead to binding contractual safeguards…Using Meta’s services to reach audiences or advertise should not mean granting wider rights to exploit publishers’ journalism, whether collected from websites or uploaded to its platforms. Publishers must retain control over additional uses of their content, including for AI, and the ability to negotiate licenses and payment.”.

    This story has been updated to include a statement from Marsha Blackburn.

    #146877. The New York Times is adding more AI features to its Cooking app, and people aren’t thrilled

    📅 28 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1135 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Niemanlab ↗ Open Full Page

    The New York Times is adding more AI features to its Cooking app, and people aren’t thrilled

    📅 28 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1135 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Niemanlab

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing.
    • Industry observers note that we will never sell your address.
    • Recent findings suggest that we have sent a confirmation link to .
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    Industry observers note that we will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    Recent findings suggest that we have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    Sometimes, adding just one upcoming ingredient to a stew can ruin the whole thing.11Olives, yecch. And that’s how at least some New York Times readers see its addition of AI features to its popular Cooking app.

    Here’s Genevieve Ko, NYT Cooking senior editor and columnist, explaining the new features:.

    I naïvely assumed A.I. wouldn’t affect my work as a recipe developer and my role at NYT Cooking, where I oversee the editorial side of our recipes and related stories. But as artificial intelligence improved, our product and engineering colleagues saw its potential to help us create features Cooking consumers wanted.

    The Times had previously rolled out AI features aimed at converting volume-based and weight-based measurements (“What’s one cup of bok choy in grams?”) and scaling a recipe up or down to serve more or fewer people. The main upcoming feature is focused on ingredient substitutions.

    Say you’re cooking braised white beans and greens with parmesan, NYT Cooking app in hand. But you notice that you’re out of chard and only have spinach. Cooking veterans know that chard is a rough-and-tumble green that has some backbone22There’s a reason one type of chard is known as “perpetual spinach.”, while spinach is a comparative wimp that will wilt the moment you look at it funny. If you need to sub in spinach for chard, how would the recipe change? Would you, for instance, add the spinach later than you would the chard to account for its pathetic stamina? That’s the sort of thing the latest AI feature could account for.

    Industry observers note that cooking staffers “spent countless hours evaluating sample after sample to get the chatbot answers to closely align with how we would answer as culinary experts,” Ko writes. “We applied the same rigor as we do to editing, grounded in Times standards.”.

    But because Ko knows that any AI-powered features are likely to be controversial with a Times audience, she spends quite a lot of space addressing potential objections, everything from “the impact of data centers” to “the concentration of power among A.I. companies” and “the risk of A.I. escaping our control.” These features are designed to enable “the tactile physical pleasure of cooking” and getting a “very real, very human creation” on your table.

    Broadly speaking, commenters weren’t buying it.

    “What a massive disappointment,” wrote Susan from New Jersey. “The internet is full of AI cooking content. I pay you because I prefer mine done by people.”.

    Industry observers note that “This decision misses the mark by such a wide margin it’s baffling,” notes Ian from Los Angeles. “And the disclosure just as baffling. It would not be inaccurate to summarize the piece as saying ‘I know doing this is bad and I don’t want to be associated with the bad thing so that’s why we are doing the bad thing.'”.

    In a recent development, “Nobody wants this, it’s bad for cooking, it’s bad for the NYT,” writes Bill from Pittsburgh. “Wasting a column trying to gaslight yourself and your audience into believing that it’s anything but is an embarrassment and a waste of everyone’s time.”.

    “PLEASE PLEASE PLEASE DO NOT DO THIS,” indicates Judah Mann of New York. “Oh, wait, you already did. Ok, I’m out.”.

    Or as Naomi from California puts it: “I am sad that AI has breached the one online resource I truly love.”.

    Because I enjoy the irony, I scraped the 171 comments left on the Times’ announcement and asked Codex (running GPT-6.1 Sol, at medium thinking) to do some sentiment analysis. (Twelve of the 171 were comments left by Times staffers; I’m excluding them here.) Roughly 77% of the reader comments were negative about the new AI features, it found, versus 14% positive and the remainder neutral or mixed. Among the biggest categories of complaint: This shouldn’t require AI. AI is destroying the environment. AI is not why I’m paying the Times $390 a year. The adjustments the AI produces are going to be bad.

    It has been revealed that dozens of commenters asked for a way to turn off the feature. “No, not at this time,” Ko responded, “though this feature is completely optional to use.” Indeed: Don’t ask AI to substitute your chard and AI won’t substitute your chard.

    Recent findings suggest that one consistent thread was that cooking is supposed to present you with difficulties and challenges and the whole point is figuring them out by yourself. “Anyone using AI for cooking has no sense of taste and no desire to work out the intricacies of cooking and baking,” writes Michael King from Brooklyn. “To use AI for recipes is beyond the pale. If you are going to use AI, then just cut to the chase and defenestrate yourself.” Or BJ from North Carolina: “So, you’re telling me that I’m too stupid to figure it out on my own?”.

    Meanwhile, the few positive comments tended to focus on how the AI feature had, in fact, made dietary substitutions easier for them. “I love the latest AI feature because it swiftly (and so far) accurately converts recipes to gluten free,” Anne Wagner from Kansas City writes. “I don’t cook for stress relief,” says Andy from San Francisco. “I cook to put dinner on the table. Anything that makes the process a little faster or smoother is welcome.”.

    Sources indicate that about six in 10 Americans remarked they have at least “some” confidence that news organizations will report the upcoming midterm election results accurately, according to a latest national survey. But only 32% said they had “quite a bit” or “a great deal” of confidence that journalists would do the job.

    In the survey from Medill Local News Initiative and the Alliance for Trust in Media, 37% mentioned they had either “not too much confidence” or “no confidence at all” that news outlets would accurately report the election results.

    Recent findings suggest that the survey was completed by a nationally representative sample of 1,057 U.S. adults either online or by telephone earlier this month. The findings echo other national surveys, including a Gallup survey that showed trust in media to report “fully, accurately, and fairly” at 33% — an increase from an all-time low last year.

    The Medill/Alliance survey found about half of Americans said they had “not too much confidence” or “no confidence at all” in news outlets to investigate voter fraud claims thoroughly. U.S. President Donald Trump has cast doubt on elections on 70% of days since returning to office — starting with false claims about voter fraud on the first day of his second term.

    According to recent reports, in another bleak result from the same poll, slightly more survey respondents stated journalists manipulate the news for political or commercial purposes than report it accurately. Across the survey, Democrats reported being more confident in (and trusting of) news organizations than Republicans. Nearly 80% of Republicans said journalists try to manipulate the news compared to 38% of independents and 24% of Democrats.

    More on the survey, conducted by NORC at the University of Chicago, here.

    #146869. Press Forward gave $20 million to 205 local newsrooms over two years. Here’s how some of them spent it.

    📅 29 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 22m • 📚 Deep Dive (4378 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Niemanlab ↗ Open Full Page

    Press Forward gave $20 million to 205 local newsrooms over two years. Here’s how some of them spent it.

    📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 22 min read (4378 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Niemanlab

    ⏱️ ~22 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing.
    • We have sent a confirmation link to .
    • The unrestricted funding helped small outlets plug holes and try newly introduced things, but publishers ran up against the limits of what two $50,000 grants could accomplish, especially when it came to hiring.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    The unrestricted funding helped small outlets plug holes and try newly introduced things, but publishers ran up against the limits of what two $50,000 grants could accomplish, especially when it came to hiring.

    In a recent development, most local newsrooms in the U.S. have one thing in common: They need more money, and many dream of dollars they can use however they want.

    RELATED ARTICLEPress Forward awards $20 million to 205 small local newsroomsSophie CulpepperOctober 16, 2024In 2024, Press Forward, the nonprofit trying to mobilize a philanthropic army for local news, declared it would give at least 100 small local newsrooms — those with annual budgets under $1 million — just that type of unrestricted funding. Almost 1,000 newsrooms applied. Ultimately, Press Forward distributed $20 million to 205 outlets. Most of them received $100,000 each, split over two years.

    It has been revealed that I wondered what the recipients had done with the money, and which problems it had (or hadn’t) solved. Between May and October, I spoke or emailed with more than 30 grantees.

    Sources indicate that the grantees represented every U.S. state, came from cities, suburbs, and rural areas, and published in multiple languages. They included for-profits and nonprofits, print and digital-only publications, college newsrooms, and public radio stations. Statewide newsrooms with fully staffed teams like The Maine Monitor, scrappy news startups like 285 South, and community newspapers powered by freelancers and part-time staff like the Copper River Record in Alaska all received funding.

    Industry observers note that for many newsrooms, Press Forward was the first grant they’d ever applied for. “Many of the country’s newsrooms are small, and few get foundation grants,” stated Press Forward executive director Dale Anglin. The open call was designed to change that and to distribute the money promptly. Grantees were required to complete two LION sustainability audits a year apart; Press Forward is analyzing that data now and will release its findings next month.1.

    RELATED ARTICLEA study of nonprofit newsrooms reveals some cracks in the model’s foundationSeth C. LewisOctober 6, 2026“People tell me that what Press Forward did was unusual and rare within philanthropy,” stated María José Ramírez Braiz, founder and CEO of Midwest-based grantee Te Lo Cuento News.

    Sources indicate that “They said to us at the beginning of the grant period, before the shit hit the fan with the federal government, ‘If you need this money to keep the lights on, keep the lights on,'” said Copper River Record editor Allison Sayer, one of the paper’s two part-time staffers. “I feel that this was really a gift.”.

    In a recent development, first-time grant applicants and recipients, in particular, noted Press Forward’s recognition gave them credibility and visibility with other funders. And publishers described the funding as a morale boost that validated low-paid work.

    Recent findings suggest that “It has been a life-changer, a lifesaver for us,” said Gretchen Sporleder Orr, who publishes the World Journal in southern Colorado with her husband. Her voice broke when she talked to me about the funding. “I don’t know if we would be in business right now if it wasn’t for the Press Forward money.”.

    The Real WV “would not still exist without Press Forward,” said Stephen Baldwin, the site’s volunteer publisher. (He’s also the former minority leader for the West Virginia Senate and a pastor of two churches.) The outlet was one of eight grantees that received just two $25,000 grants over two years. “There’s not exactly a lot of capital floating around West Virginia for nonprofit news,” Baldwin said, “and without this outside impact, we wouldn’t be able to do this work.” But he hopes that the site can be less reliant on grants in the future.

    It has been revealed that the funding did not save every recipient. One grantee, Atlanta Civic Circle, shut down earlier this year. Atlanta Civic Circle did not receive its second $50,000 grant because it didn’t complete the first LION audit, Anglin said. (Atlanta Civic Circle did not respond to my request for an interview, but executive director Saba Long wrote on LinkedIn in June that “the funding environment for local nonprofit journalism is extraordinarily difficult right now.”) Other recipients have merged or transformed since applying for the grant.2.

    In a recent development, RELATED ARTICLEFrom bad to worse: 2026 is shaping up to be “a super El Niño year for local news”Sophie CulpepperOctober 13, 2026Medill’s annual State of Local News report, released this month, describes a local news ecosystem in a “state of precarity.” That state of precariousness helps explain how $100,000 over two years can be a “godsend,” a “miracle,” and not enough. As one grantee put it, “Right now, these are shanties built on a beach, waiting for a hurricane to come through.”.

    “Press Forward reached newsrooms that don’t have existing relationships with major national funders,” mentioned Nina Ignaczak, the founder, publisher, and editor of Planet Detroit. “The challenge now is whether the commitment holds.”.

    The funding helped newsrooms keep the lights on, whether they used it to pay bills, pay down debt, make payroll, or as a buffer when something went wrong.

    It has been revealed that “The flexibility that Press Forward has given us has allowed us to fill — I wouldn’t say emergencies, but unexpected gaps,” said Richard Young, founder and executive director of CivicLex in Kentucky. It brought on a consulting editor to keep city hall coverage going after losing a reporter, and purchased upcoming software. Without the funding, CivicLex likely would have had to dip into its reserves, he said.

    Bob Bonnar, publisher of the News Letter Journal in Wyoming, used the first payment from Press Forward to upgrade computers and cameras and give some staffers raises. “That chewed up the money very quickly,” he mentioned, “and I probably should have held some of it back because the News Letter Journal ended up having a pretty rough year in 2025.” He had to use about half of the second $50,000 payment to repay an operating loan. The rest covered the remaining revenue shortfall and kept the organization in the black through the winter.

    Vandana Kumar, publisher of the California-based ethnic media outlet India Currents, described the funding as a “stabilizing force” that allowed the newsroom to keep operating despite a contraction in philanthropic giving and cuts to local government advertising.

    The Copper River Record built infrastructure to host digital ads and created a newly introduced website. It held listening sessions with Native villages in its coverage area and donated subscriptions to local Tribal offices. It improved the design of its print newspaper. Sayer paid freelancers to complete Press Pass training and pursued other professional development. And she was able to take on more ambitious stories about PFAS and “forever chemicals.”.

    Sources indicate that the Press Forward funding was “the biggest single windfall in nearly 20 years for our small community newspaper,” Sandpoint Reader publisher Ben Olson told me. The Idaho-based paper used the money to travel to the state capital for Press Club awards and design a latest media kit, which Olson said has improved ad sales. The Reader also paid a large chunk of its printing bill, paid its rent a year in advance, and gave staffers bonuses. (The bonuses helped the paper become 100% employee-owned; Olson’s two employees bought in when Olson’s business partner and co-owner retired.).

    Industry observers note that the open-ended nature of the grants gave Colorado’s World Journal “the flexibility to be able to make a change, do a thing, and then pivot as needed,” Sporleder Orr mentioned. “When we were in the toilet, all I could think about was, like, ‘Is there going to be anything in the post office today so that I can make payroll?’ ‘Oh, my God, we’ve got to pay rent.’” Sometimes she and her husband skipped their own paychecks to pay staff. The grant gave them “emotional bandwidth” to strategy ahead.

    Many grantees used the funding to hire full- or part-time staffers. Sometimes, that worked out well.

    The Mānoa Mirror, an online newsroom based at the University of Hawaii at Mānoa, received two $25,000 grants, which it used to hire a managing editor, a student editorial coordinator, three student reporters, and a social media producer. (The managing editor was paid a stipend, and the other positions were part-time.) The work had previously depended on “faculty goodwill and volunteerism, which was not sustainable for long,” mentioned Hye-ryeon Lee, who was professor and chair of the school of communication and information until retiring this summer. With the new hires, the site went from publishing a few stories a month to publishing daily.

    The Real WV’s first LION audit pointed to a need its small team had already recognized: hiring someone to sell ads. It hired a public school teacher with sales experience (including selling ads for the yearbook) part-time.

    Sources indicate that the funding allowed Te Lo Cuento News to pay contributors consistently and to add contract, part-time positions including a sales manager, an office administrator, and a couple of reporters. The only position it could sustain beyond the grant period is the part-time sales manager, Ramírez Braiz stated.

    Industry observers note that the Texas Spur is one of five weekly newspapers owned by Paragraph Ranch Media. Originally, the team planned to use the Press Forward grant to secure a loan to improve company housing and hire a journalist based in Spur (population 863 as of 2020). But nobody took the newspaper up on the free housing offer, mentioned editor and general manager Barbara Brannon. So the company hired four early-career journalists (two full-time, two part-time) living in its 10-county coverage area. Three of the four left for jobs in other industries halfway through their second year. The one who stayed is doing well as a regional sports reporter, Brannon said, and a hire who replaced a person who left is now managing editor for The Post Dispatch.3.

    The turnover Brannon experienced isn’t unique to Spur. Other newsrooms also found hiring with grant money challenging.

    Sometimes, that was because of location. “Had we been able to find the right people from the outset, I believe the grant would have had a greater impact on the business,” said Anton Kaufer, regional publisher for Hagadone Media Montana. In rural Northwest Montana, though, recruiting and retaining staff is a challenge, and Hagadone’s Mineral Independent struggled to replace its salesperson and office manager after they retired. The experience “reinforced for us that sustainability isn’t just about having the funding,” Kaufer said. “It’s also about having the people in place to make the most of it.”.

    The World Journal tried placing an ad for a salesperson with the Colorado Press Association and got “absolutely no interest,” Sporleder Orr mentioned. “People living in northern Colorado don’t particularly want to come live in a teeny-tiny town in a rural, broke part of the state.” (She credited the grant with giving her the mental space to fire a salesperson who wasn’t working out, then regroup.).

    According to recent reports, other times, the money just wasn’t enough. “The reality is that $100,000 over two years isn’t a lot,” one grantee who asked to stay anonymous told me. “You can’t hire somebody with that.”.

    In a recent development, ecoRI’s experience illustrates those limitations. Before receiving the Press Forward grant, EcoRI had used other grant funding and reserves to hire a director of development in a one-year contract position. In its grant application to Press Forward, the team proposed converting that role into a full-time staff position with benefits.

    Sources indicate that the salary limited the hiring pool, though. The development director position paid $65,000 a year, which “is really not the market rate for a director of development” in the area, publisher and cofounder Jo Detz mentioned. (She said it should be more like $90,000.) The staffer they ended up hiring came from another state and hadn’t worked in news before. In a staff position, he cost more than he was bringing in. Detz laid him off and eliminated the position last December. She called the experience “heartbreaking.”.

    “At the point where I knew this wasn’t working,” she noted, “there wasn’t enough runway to pivot, rethink, rehire.”.

    Beyond the salary limitations, Detz thinks the development director didn’t have enough runway to succeed. The kind of development the staffer was hired to oversee — major gifts and individual giving — is a long game; “that position would need at least two or three years to begin to see some benefits,” she said. Now, she’s back where she started, juggling fundraising with her other work.

    “I know it’s crazy to say that $100,000 over two years wasn’t enough,” she said, “but it was not enough to make a meaningful difference to our revenue strategy.”.

    In a recent development, planet Detroit’s Ignaczak was in a unique position: Around the same time the newsroom received the Press Forward grant, Planet Detroit also received a $500,000 three-year grant from the MacArthur Foundation. That grant allowed her to hire a managing editor, she said.

    Sources indicate that ignaczak believes general operating support is what small nonprofit newsrooms need. But to be effective, “I really think fully funding a revenue role for a minimum of three years is what needs to happen to build sustainability, if that is the goal,” she noted. “And $100,000 over two years is not enough to achieve that.”.

    Industry observers note that notiVisión Georgia, a Spanish-language local news outlet with one full-time staffer, is committed to print in a world moving away from it. The print newspaper is the only way the outlet has been able to use to “generate real economic value,” mentioned CEO Mónica Pirela, because it’s where local companies want to place ads. The organization spent some of its Press Forward funds on printing and distribution. Pirela wears “every hat” right now, and the organization’s top need is a dedicated sales manager, she said.

    California’s BenitoLink, meanwhile, used some of the Press Forward funding to begin printing in 2025. That will allow it to apply for newspaper of record status and get paid for running legal notices.

    According to recent reports, in Minnesota, Swift County Monitor-News publisher and owner Reed Anfinson called the grant a “godsend” at a time when tariffs and rising gas prices have driven up printing and delivery costs and weakened advertisers’ budgets. The for-profit Monitor-News put some of its Press Forward funding toward redesigning its print newspaper. Anfinson also purchased materials as part of an “Out of Sight/Out of Mind” advertising campaign stressing the value of print. (He created the campaign himself, using Midjourney for the images.) For news organizations in small towns, Anfinson believes, digital revenue will never be enough to sustain operations.

    Some organizations used the funding to expand their remit beyond news.

    Recent findings suggest that for instance, the Copper River Record partnered with the Copper River Native Association to include weekly language graphics in the paper for Ahtna, a critically endangered language, coordinating with a local kindergarten class. That project required a lot of time and investment up front, Sayer said, but it can continue beyond the life of the grant.

    Industry observers note that planet Detroit used some Press Forward funding for reporting, but “the most significant thing the grant made possible wasn’t any single story,” Ignaczak stated. The grant gave the team time to work on its Civic Action Toolbox, which turns reporting into civic engagement prompts. In a story about a local ballot proposal, for instance, the embedded toolbox flags upcoming public meetings, links to contact information for local representatives, and suggests an organization to follow. The tool is also in beta testing with other newsrooms.

    Recent findings suggest that “The whole project came from having the space to ask what our readers actually need from us beyond information, and then building toward that,” Ignaczak said. “Unrestricted funding makes that kind of work possible.”.

    Industry observers note that anfinson of the Monitor-News took the unusual step of writing a grant application on behalf of the local school district, which was losing students to adjacent districts. He used some of the Press Forward funding to match a $2,500 grant to the district. The district then ran $5,000 in ads in a “goodwill effort” to stem declining enrollment. The partnership helped to raise the Monitor-News’s profile, he remarked, by highlighting the benefits of newspaper advertising.

    Press Forward required grantees to complete two LION sustainability audits. But it also offered optional coaching via the media consulting tech giant Blue Engine to help implement the first audit’s recommendations. Of the 205 grantees, 154 participated in coaching, Anglin said.

    The coaching kicked off in January, with most individual coaches and grantees meeting monthly. Multiple participants stated the support would have been more beneficial if it were introduced earlier. This was a tradeoff of Press Forward moving promptly to get money out the door, Anglin said.4.

    Industry observers note that this was the first large, unrestricted grant Austin Common had ever received, and it struggled with how to spend the money. “It felt like a lot of pressure,” mentioned Amy Stansbury, the site’s editor-in-chief and only full-time staffer.

    Stansbury wanted to bring on the organization’s first full-time employees, but didn’t want to make those hires (and spend all the grant money) until she had a clear blueprint. The coaching helped her figure out which hires made the most strategic sense and how to budget for them.

    According to recent reports, A few publishers were lukewarm about the substance of the coaching, but the majority I heard from were enthusiastic. At first, Baldwin was skeptical and worried the coaching might amount to “checking a box.” In practice, though, he stated it’s been “tremendously helpful” for tasks like writing the job description for the Real WV’s sales position.

    Recent findings suggest that sporleder Orr called the coaching “incredible.” The monthly sessions helped her with everything from tackling grant proposals to improving her Google Analytics skills. The combination of money and coaching, she added, “makes sure that the recipients don’t just continue doing business as usual.”.

    It has been revealed that in addition to the funding, Press Forward paid for grantees to attend conferences. Anglin stated 111 grantees attended the Lenfest News Philanthropy Summit in Philadelphia in 2025, 81 attended the same conference (which I also attended) in 2026, and 87 attended the Business of Local conference in Salt Lake City in 2025. A handful of grantees attended affinity conferences.

    In a recent development, stansbury found attending conferences for the first time helpful and eye-opening. It taught her “there’s this secret shadow world of [invitation-only] foundation and grant funding.” Press Forward’s travel support to attend a national conference was “transformative” for India Currents, Kumar said, giving it visibility and access to relationship-building.

    To small newsrooms, the grant felt like a Press Forward stamp of approval that put them on the map for other funders. The Mirror’s Lee called the Press Forward funding “instrumental” in securing a $20,000 grant from a local foundation. But that was an exception among publishers I heard from; most didn’t feel the visibility and credibility conferred by the grant directly translated to other funders giving them more money.

    Recent findings suggest that so several publishers, including Ramírez Braiz of Te Lo Cuento News, would like to see Press Forward go a step further and make individual introductions to funders. “Those more personal introductions can make a major difference for small organizations,” she said.

    Ramírez Braiz also called for “more shared learning around outcomes and impact.” Few grantees had a good sense of what others in the cohort were up to, and some were interested in more knowledge sharing with peer organizations, though the day-to-day grind of keeping one’s own newsroom running was a common impediment.

    Industry observers note that since 2023, Anglin said, Press Forward’s network of more than 130 funders has invested $258 million directly in newsrooms. That suggests that over half of the more than $400 million the coalition states it’s invested has gone to newsrooms.

    Industry observers note that when Press Forward first announced the direct funding for newsrooms, it “felt really awesome,” the grantee who asked to stay anonymous told me. To the grantee, it was meaningful to see Press Forward give funding to more organizations than planned in response to the scale of need. But when Press Forward went on to a second funding round in which single organizations, including both newsrooms and newsroom-adjacent organizations like the International Women’s Media Foundation and LION, received as much as $1.5 million for infrastructure projects, the same grantee noted it felt like “a slap in the face.”.

    “Many of the problems newsrooms face aren’t unique to them individually,” Anglin said. “If we are attempting to solve problems at scale, we have to intervene not just at the newsroom level, but at the systems level, too.” She said that because many of the infrastructure grantees serve multiple newsrooms, “investing in them creates a multiplier effect across the industry.”.

    Sources indicate that the argument that funding support organizations and infrastructure lifts more boats is “a cop-out,” this publisher mentioned. “I think the philanthropists know it, I think the associations know it, and I think the potential grantees that are not funders or associations or intermediaries know it.”.

    Young had a different perspective. Because of CivicLex’s broad scope, it seeks out funding from both democracy funders and journalism funders. Young thinks local news funders are way ahead on getting dollars into local communities.

    According to recent reports, “I think Press Forward has done one of the more effective jobs of anything I’ve seen in the broader landscape of my world, and the civic renewal space, of delivering resources to the local level,” he said. (He added, “No one is ever happy in the local news ecosystem when I say that folks in the local news ecosystem don’t know how good they have it. That does not win me a lot of friends.”).

    Most publishers I heard from see grants like this as critical to continued operation, yet they’re wary of overreliance on philanthropy.

    Young said he’d be surprised if local news is still a focus for national philanthropy in eight years. “Filling your cup up with money that will be impossible to recover in four years is a danger zone,” he added.

    Sources indicate that right now, more than 80% of Planet Detroit’s revenue mix comes from foundations. Ignaczak stated the organization hopes to bring that down to 50% by 2028. “But for nonprofit newsrooms covering environmental and public health complications in a mid-size metro, general operating grants aren’t a crutch,” she said. “They’re infrastructure.”.

    Industry observers note that as for Press Forward, “Time will tell, as these grants go away, what impact [they’ve] actually had on the newsrooms that received [them], how many have managed to build sustainability,” she added. “I think a newsroom that needed $50,000 to survive to next year had problems that $50,000 isn’t going to solve.”.

    LOOKOUT executive director Jake Hylton believes there’s enough funding to go around. “While there may not be enough to support every single newsroom at a very large amount,” he noted, “I do believe that there is a larger investment in news that could be done.”.

    Recent findings suggest that A second grantee who asked to stay anonymous was blunt about their fears for the future. “We’re scared shitless about 2027,” this person said, “because not only is the Press Forward money not returning, we also see none of the national grants that sustained us in 2024 and previous years.”.

    It has been revealed that the Copper River Record was in the black before receiving this grant, and the lean paper’s fixed overhead remains low. For the Record, Press Forward has been like “a fairy godmother,” Sayer stated.

    According to recent reports, “I’m not going to lie: I will miss having the money to say yes to any reasonable story,” she continued. “But I think that, even going back to our original budget, the strength of what we learned will continue to help us deliver a higher quality paper that is more relevant to the communities we serve.”.

    The Sandpoint Reader, Olson noted, is “surviving” right now. “We’d love to be thriving,” he added, “but we’re happy to continue to survive when many print publications aren’t.” He credited the Press Forward grant with giving the burned-out team “the chance to fall in love with our industry again.”.

    Sporleder Orr feels nervous about what’s ahead, but with the World Journal in a much more comfortable cash flow position, she and her husband are “in a way better mental state about the business.”.

    Recent findings suggest that “We feel good about the future right now, that we are going to be able to keep going and make it,” she said. “We’re back to, ‘This is what we do ’til we die.'”.
