    College football already has an Orange Bowl, a Peach Bowl, and a Citrus Bowl, so on its face, there’s nothing outlandish about the concept of an Onion Bowl.

    But this matchup wouldn’t be titled to evoke some locale’s bumper crop, à la the Famous Idaho Potato Bowl. Instead it would market “America’s Finest News Source,” The Onion. (Today’s top headlines: Bain Capital Acquires Tibetan Buddhism For $35 Million; Abdul El-Sayed Makes History As First Physically Healthy Senator; Chuck Schumer Delivers Victory Speech To Previously Enthusiastic Crowd.).

    On Thursday morning, Onion CEO (and past Nieman Lab contributor) Ben Collins unveiled the publication’s quest to buy naming rights for a bowl game, both on Bluesky and on the podcast Pablo Torre Finds Out:.

    The Onion is extremely close to buying an honest-to-goodness, Division 1 college football bowl series bowl game.

    Yes, we're trying to pull off The Onion Bowl.

    A few days before Christmas, potentially in Texas.

    Sources indicate that but we've already been banned once. And we need your help.

    — Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:32 AM.

    For those unfamiliar, American college football seasons traditionally end with a few dozen bowl games, scattered around the country (and occasionally outside it). Nearly all of these games sell naming rights to one organization or another, leading to fun combinations like the Poulan Weed Eater Independence Bowl, the TaxSlayer.com Gator Bowl, and the Union Home Mortgage Gasparilla Bowl. Collins wants to buy the rights to one of the several bowl games that are still without a sponsor for their games next month.

    This absurdity — though no more absurd, I suppose, than the Snoop Dogg Arizona Bowl presented by Gin & Juice by Dre and Snoop — serves as the excellent marketing hook to get people to buy a $75/year print subscription, a major driver of The Onion’s revenue.

    Industry observers note that indeed, only three U.S. newspapers have a daily print circulation over 100,000 — The Wall Street Journal, The New York Times, and the New York Post; The Washington Post and USA Today have already fallen below that line. (At the risk of being pedantic, though, The Onion appears in print monthly, not daily, making it a bit of an apples-to-oranges comparison. Also, The Onion gets to make up its stories.).

    Collins states The Onion actually got quite close to buying the naming rights to the Fresh Orleans Bowl, which last year lost its longtime naming sponsor, the…Ohio-based freight-shipping concern R+L Carriers? The Onion was prepared to pay “mid six figures.” But the organization that runs the bowl, the Greater New Orleans Sports Foundation, apparently remarked no deep into the process, a move Collins attributed to “politics.” (I reached out to the Greater New Orleans Sports Foundation for comment — a sentence I did not expect to type today — but did not hear back.).

    So the guys who sell bowl games ushered us to what we thought was a pretty good fit: The New Orleans Bowl.

    According to recent reports, I love New Orleans. I love having crawfish out of the back of a pickup truck at 3 a.m. The game would've been in the Superdome two days before Christmas. Good fit! Right? Right???

    — Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:38 AM.

    Then the folks who run the Upcoming Orleans Bowl, a commission that includes representatives of the city and state of Louisiana, found out our plans to highlight our mascot:.

    — Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:39 AM.

    Despite getting all approvals from ESPN and scraping together the cash, right as we were about to sign the paper work to put The Onion Sports Bowl in Fresh Orleans, their state-funded commission called us and noted it straight up: "No.".

    We asked why. They said politics. And the Sickos Guy.

    #146838. WordPress 7.2 Arrives Dec. 8 – Last-Minute Changes Still Being Made via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2680 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Searchenginejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    WordPress 7.2 Arrives Dec. 8 – Last-Minute Changes Still Being Made via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2680 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • This version has, in beta, turned on a newly introduced public address on updated sites.
    • In a recent development, this feature is on by default.
    • In a recent development, that makes /random/ the 7.2 change most sites will need to decide on before updating.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    WordPress 7.2 is due on Dec. 8. This version has, in beta, turned on a newly introduced public address on updated sites. /random/ directs you to a random published post. Versions of the address also do this within categories, tags, author archives, or eligible custom post types.

    In a recent development, this feature is on by default. Switching it off will require coding, as there are no settings available via the WordPress dashboard to disable this feature. Further, in the November roundup of the WordPress Developer Blog, the filter name listed doesn’t match the actual filter name used in the code. Copying the name from the Developer Blog will have no effect.

    In a recent development, that makes /random/ the 7.2 change most sites will need to decide on before updating. The new Secrets API, a way for plugins to store credentials, was removed from 7.2 on Nov. 17. That came days after Matt Mullenweg, who leads the release, sided with a request to pull it.

    Core’s latest AI pieces are tools for developers and plugins, and none of them adds an AI feature visitors or editors will see.

    Recent findings suggest that beta five is the latest test release, and WordPress notes not to run it on production sites. The first release candidate (RC1) is due Nov. 17, so details can still change before the final release.

    Aaron Jorbin’s developer note opens, “A request to example.com/random/ will lead end owners to a randomly selected published post. The feature is on by default.”.

    The /random/ path and its category, tag, author, and post type versions use the default base with pretty permalinks. The base is translatable, and a newly introduced field on the Permalinks screen changes it. The development code also responds to a random query variable, so ?random works too on the home page and archives. Since a Nov. 16 change, a search URL that includes it redirects to the same search without the parameter.

    According to recent reports, by default, posts are eligible. Pages and attachments aren’t. Custom post types are considered eligible if they’re publicly queryable, have archives and the developer hasn’t registered them with 'randomable' => false. The code filters for only published posts (with no password).

    In a recent development, it uses a 302 redirect. The development code sends no-cache headers and includes the header X-Robots-Tag: noindex, follow with the 302 redirect response. This header covers the original /random/ request, but not the post this redirects to. If there is no match to the query, the request will return a 404.

    In a recent development, if you’ve created a published page with the slug “random,” then this will override the redirect. The same thing happens if you create a post with the slug “random,” when permalinks are set to use the post name. Peter Wilson confirmed this in the comments after Daniel Iser raised it, and recommended using a base like “shuffle” instead.

    It has been revealed that random queries run from the main WP_Query, so pre_get_posts callbacks that change archives will also affect their random redirect. Developers wishing to target random requests only should use wp_is_random_content_query().

    In a recent development, turning this feature off is done by adding the one-line mu-plugin shown in the note, add_filter( 'wp_enable_random_content_redirect', '__return_false' );. This will prevent WordPress from generating rewrite rules for random content, hide the base field on the Permalinks screen, and ignore the query variable. The code’s documentation indicates that flushing the rewrite rules is necessary after changing the filter value.

    The roundup’s version, wp_enable_random_content_direct, isn’t used anywhere in the code.

    Random redirects made their initial appearance in the code on Sept. 21; at this point they were an optional ?random query that needed sites to return true for a filter called enable_random_content_redirect if they wanted them to be active.

    They were reverted two days after that. The commit message remarked of the feature, “The feature is intended to land in WordPress 7.2 but will need some work.”.

    In a recent development, on Oct. 16, they returned as /random/ rewrite rules turned on, with the filter name changed and the default for the filter set to true. They were added to Beta 1 on Oct. 20.

    It has been revealed that jorbin’s post drew a long thread of objections. Joost de Valk wrote, “This is a horrible idea to turn on by default.” In a later reply, he added, “Now I fear people will randomly end up on invoices, offers, client specific pages, etc.” Responding to another commenter, Jorbin wrote, “The WordPress Philosophies mean that opt-out options are not added for every feature, otherwise the options pages would become unusable.”.

    Mullenweg replied to a commenter whose site already has a page named “random,” writing, “I agree it should not use page URL structure.” In a separate comment, he wrote, “I don’t think this should be an appended pretty URL; the request was just for /?random, just at root.” He also addressed concerns about performance and exposure, saying query strings, searches, and REST calls offer “far more ways” to exhaust a site’s resources.

    As of Nov. 17, no one maintaining the feature had posted a change to its default or its URL structure. Since the note, code changes from Nov. 12 to Nov. 17 have adjusted when the redirect fires, how it treats searches and how it picks a post.

    See also: Web Almanac Data Reveals CMS Plugins Are Setting Technical SEO Standards (Not SEOs).

    The Secrets API would have allowed plugins to save API keys, tokens and more via libsodium encryption, and would have utilized the options tables, which hosts could replace with their own keyring or storage utilizing a secrets.php drop-in.

    Sources indicate that wordPress reverted the API on Nov. 17. The commit points to feedback on the announcement that questioned the design, including whether one API should both write secrets and read the ones a host supplies. Peter Wilson had also found that the API never checked its manage_secrets and manage_network_secrets capabilities when secrets were set. The commit message opens, “Removes the Secrets API from WordPress 7.2 to allow more time for the API to mature before it ships in a future release.”.

    Earlier, Ryan McCue, a contributor, had commented that he believes secrets managed outside WordPress should only be readable and never writable to WordPress and that allowing writes to be part of this feature and easy to accomplish makes the API “likely to ossify” around that design. He argued that, under this design, a secrets store backed by hardware security modules offered no additional protection over an already encrypted database. He concluded, “I am a strong -1 on this feature, and I think this should be backed out of core for 7.2 until the above is resolved.”.

    Mullenweg replied, “I agree with @rmccue here.” Two minutes later, he wrote, “It’s also not a great time to be making ourselves a target for very sensitive things like that.”.

    In a recent development, eric Mann, the writer of the developer note, responded to the encryption point, writing, “Encryption at rest protects against someone walking off with the disk. It does nothing about SQL injection, a leaked mysqldump, a misconfigured backup bucket.” Mann initially wanted to leave the API in 7.2 and referenced a proposed solution for how the AI plugin handles failed write operations, one of the items that was mentioned by McCue.

    After Wilson’s finding, Mann replied, “I’m not excited about it but agree more time will help us ship a more solid foundation here. I’d still like to target at least 7.3 if possible.”.

    In a recent development, the AI plugin version 1.5.0 (released Oct. 29) moved its opt-in Key Encryption experiment into a bundled version of the Secrets API which stores the plugin’s AI service keys. Its maintainers had a pull request open to upgrade it to the version planned for core. After the revert, Jeffrey Paul, who had approved it, wrote that the plugin should “use an approach here that leverages the functionality outside of core” instead. The pull request was still open on Nov. 17, and 1.5.0 was still the latest release.

    See also: When The WordPress Plugin Update Is The Security Risk: Why SEOs Should Pay Attention.

    According to recent reports, wordPress put AI building blocks into core before this release. Roger Montti reported in May that 7.0 shipped four of them, including the WP AI Client and a Connectors screen for AI services. In October, he reported that WordPress had released a canonical MCP Adapter plugin for connecting AI systems through the Model Context Protocol (MCP).

    WordPress 7.2 is set to add three latest read-only abilities, which are registered actions called by other applications. The new read-only abilities allow other applications to query content, consumers, and WordPress settings. A developer will be able to build an embedding, a numeric representation of text, through the AI client to provide similarity search functionality.

    In addition to adding the three read-only abilities, the WordPress core team has marked those abilities as exposed to clients such as the WordPress core REST API, MCP, or AI agents. According to the documentation, “Exposure flags do not grant execution permission.” The content query ability requires a logged-in user and checks if the user has read permission for the returned posts. There is currently no MCP server included in the WordPress core.

    According to a post released about version 1.5.0 of the AI plugin, the AI plugin provides versions of these fresh abilities that are expected to be identical to the versions “coming in WordPress core with 7.2 this December.” Additionally, the post states there are breaking changes in how existing integrations work because of this revision.

    Recent findings suggest that the AI features editors will experience live within the AI plugin itself, where they are at the moment being tested as opt-in experiments with different requirements; two examples include text-to-speech and revision summaries where content is sent to the site’s selected AI provider. In addition, Content Verification identifies C2PA Content Credentials, a standard for providing provenance information for digital media. However, according to the release post, Content Verification “does not yet perform cryptographic verification” of C2PA Content Credentials. Another feature, MCP Access, decides what the plugin makes available over MCP.

    The AI plugin’s screenshot reveals the “Unverified” notice displayed when Content Credentials are detected.

    In a recent development, the AI plugin flags detected Content Credentials as unverified. Screenshot: WordPress AI.

    Supporting broader types of agents in the future is part of plans for the next release. WordPress’s agentic-web proposal states, “Agents can already accomplish a lot with WordPress through WP-CLI, the REST API, and file management. However, these approaches often require local access or more advanced configurations.” The agentic-web proposal plans to implement support for WordPress 7.3 and is planning to develop foundational elements during the 7.2 cycle.

    Recent findings suggest that admin and login screens in 7.2 separate the combined JavaScript and style sheets they once had into individual assets. According to the roundup, this means each asset is loaded separately by WordPress, which has also included prefetching of the assets needed for the next screen it thinks you’ll be viewing. load-scripts.php and load-styles.php have been deprecated in this version. This change applies to the admin and login screens only.

    It has been revealed that the newly introduced SVG icons in the admin bar and menu replace the ones previously made available via the Dashicons font. So if your plugins used CSS to add additional styling to those icons’ ::before content, you may want to review them. Beta 5 introduced notification emails when an application password was created. Also according to WordPress, 7.2 aims to include full support for PHP 8.6.

    The preview below reveals the latest icons in the WordPress admin menu.

    Upcoming icons in the WordPress 7.2 admin menu. Screenshot: WordPress Developer Blog.

    Whether to keep /random/ active is probably the decision most WordPress sites will have to make by Dec. 8. Unless /random/ is turned off, all published posts without a password (including content from a custom post type that is publicly queryable with an archive) can randomly appear. Some commenters on Jorbin’s post thought that would be true for some testimonial or client page custom post types they had created, even though those are not included in the site’s navigation links. First, check which of your custom post types are publicly queryable and have an archive. Then, for any of those custom post types that shouldn’t appear, set 'randomable' => false so that they won’t show up through this method.

    The noindex header isn’t applied to the posts /random/ points to, and the selection made by WordPress doesn’t automatically skip posts an SEO plugin has set to noindex. There was still no response as of Nov. 16 to a commenter who questioned that in the developer notes. Customers of SEO plugins that prevent access to posts via search engines may want to determine if /random/ will still be able to reach those posts.

    On sites behind a page cache or CDN, /random/ can return a 404 right after the upgrade. According to the hosting team, that lasts until rewrite rules are flushed, which core does on the first wp-admin request after the upgrade, per site on multisite. On the platform the team tested, a cached 404 stayed after the upgrade until the cache was purged. One tester using shared hosting without a page cache found the rules already in place. To help prevent a stale 404 from being served, purge the page cache after the first admin visit.

    McCue raised the load that the selection’s random ordering could put on large sites, especially if bots hit /random/ repeatedly. Jorbin noted on Nov. 10 that he had opened a ticket to look at performance on very large sites, and a fix landed on Nov. 17. It looks up random post IDs instead of sorting the archive at random, a method the commit claims “keeps the cost of a request independent of the number of posts”. Archives whose posts are too sparse among the post IDs fall back to a cached pool of up to 1,000 randomly ordered posts. Building that pool still reads every eligible post. Sites with a persistent object cache can reuse the pool for 10 minutes. Mullenweg’s view is that searches and REST calls already offer more ways to strain a site. Teams with large archives can watch for repeated hits on /random/ in their logs after the revision.

    Agency managers running multiple sites will likely handle /random/ in the same way across their entire fleet using a mu-plugin with the correct spelling of the filter.

    Plugin developers can opt public post types out of /random/ where a random visit makes no sense. They’ll also want to check admin CSS for the icon change and enhancement any integration that calls the content, user, and settings abilities.

    Recent findings suggest that mullenweg’s /random/ comment about URL structure could lead to changes to the original /random/ strategy. Many commenters (on the developer note) are opposed to the default.

    According to recent reports, when the Secrets API returns, and with what design, is now open too. Sites using the AI plugin’s Key Encryption will need to see how its next release handles the revert.

    Whether /random/ will honor SEO plugins’ noindex settings is still an open question. The release date itself has two values on WordPress.org. The release schedule indicates Dec. 8, while the roadmap still lists Dec. 10.

    RC1 on Nov. 17 will include the Field Guide and the 7.2 branch. This should help identify where /random/ ended up. RC2 is set to be released Nov. 24, and RC3 Dec. 1. A dry run and code freeze for Dec. 7 precede the scheduled release on Dec. 8. Agent connection work, broader than just connecting an MCP, along with authorization work in core, is targeted for WordPress 7.3.

    To test if /random/ can access your content and how this impacts caching, you’ll need to install RC1 onto a staging version of your website.

    All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    It has been revealed that we have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    “I’m the person who’s holding the door open and being like, ‘OK, you just got here, this is what we’re talking about right now.’”.

    The data is in: News creators and influencers are a major source of news for Americans, especially people under 30. This is the latest edition of Creators of Record, an occasional series of interviews with popular creators about how they do their jobs.

    For Nikita Redkar, a major part of filming a video is putting together an outfit.

    In a recent development, in a July video about youth-led protests in India, the 33-year-old is walking around Fresh York City explaining how movements grow when people with opposing views come together on the things they do agree on. She’s wearing a white tube top and black jeans with sunglasses holding her hair back, along with a matching gold necklace and earrings that look like soda can tabs. You can’t see her shoes, but they clack enough for you to know she’s wearing a heel.

    It has been revealed that in another about comedian Shane Gillis’s Saturday Night Live monologue in which he called women “whores” for wearing shorts to the gym, she’s seated on the floor of her living room wearing a black silk velvet top with a pink faux-fur collar and sleeve cuffs. In the style of a Get Ready With Me video, she explains how 2000s comedy and pop culture entrenched misogynistic ideas of gender roles while applying her makeup.

    A full-time news creator who mostly focuses on American politics and culture through a leftist and feminist lens, Redkar calls herself a “professor at Bimbo University.” The girliness is the point, she told me.

    It has been revealed that “I want to show that you don’t have to sacrifice these parts of yourself to be taken seriously,” Redkar noted. “You should be taken seriously no matter what.”.

    In a recent development, redkar and I chatted in October about how she does her job, leaning into her femininity to explain the news, and what her relationship with social media is like. Our conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

    Hanaa’ Tameez: How did you start creating news videos? Nikita Redkar: I started in 2022, kind of accidentally. I did standup comedy for five years before the pandemic. I was always doing political humor. I took many political science classes in college, I wrote for the college newspaper, and I always had an interest in politics. In 2022, I had a video that really took off — like millions of views within a few hours. I was explaining the Russian invasion of Ukraine with a silly metaphor about Russia being a jealous ex that doesn’t want to see his ex thrive and be independent. I tried that formula again a couple weeks later…about NATO and fears of World War III. I explained exactly what would be affected. I noted there’s not going to be a world war, but things are going to get really expensive, which happened. I also used a girly friendship metaphor for that video. That’s when I started doing that formula — leaning into hyper-femininity to explain these complex geopolitical topics.

    Industry observers note that tameez: Tell me about why this work is important to you. Redkar: I feel like my work has made a lot of these daunting topics a little bit more accessible. But when I talk to my audience, I intentionally give them hope. I don’t just tell the news, but tell them, OK, if we really locked in and held these corporations and the government accountable and we were intentional in our activism, this is what the world could look like. It’s important to make information accessible because we are going through so much news-wise and not all of it is easy to understand. I enjoy bringing this information I’m naturally interested in to people in a way where everyone [can] get involved. When I was starting, I was not [a stereotypical] history buff or a news junkie. I would like to think that someone who looks like me and talks like me should be just as interested in politics and just as interested in the outcome of this country.

    It has been revealed that tameez: How do you define your niche and how did you get there? Redkar: My niche is educational. Bimbo University is a place where anyone can start no matter where they are [in their political education]. My audience [ranges from] people who are just getting into politics to people who maybe were triggered by a specific event in the news to start paying more attention to it. I feel like leftist content creators all operate on a spectrum. You have people who are getting really deep into Marxist theory, for example, and things like geopolitics. I’m at the beginning. I’m the person who’s holding the door open and being like, “OK, you just got here, this is what we’re talking about right now.”.

    Redkar: My niche is educational. Bimbo University is a place where anyone can start no matter where they are [in their political education]. My audience [ranges from] people who are just getting into politics to people who maybe were triggered by a specific event in the news to start paying more attention to it.

    Industry observers note that I feel like leftist content creators all operate on a spectrum. You have people who are getting really deep into Marxist theory, for example, and things like geopolitics. I’m at the beginning. I’m the person who’s holding the door open and being like, “OK, you just got here, this is what we’re talking about right now.”.

    According to recent reports, tameez: You’re the first news creator I’ve talked to who does Get Ready With Me videos. You take all of your interests and apply them [to your videos] to be relatable. Redkar: I got into this huge argument with my best friend’s mom, who was a second-wave feminist in the 70s and 80s. She was upset that I called my page Bimbo University. She was like, “You’re dumbing yourself down. Women shouldn’t dumb themselves down. You are just as smart as a man, if not smarter than a man.” That was my lightbulb moment of, oh, your feminism has always been to measure your worth as equal to a man and by the standards of men…working toward a man’s acceptance. In some industries, you’ve got to do that. I don’t blame [people] for thinking like that. But the reason I dial so deep into this hyper-femininity — leaning into these girly things like getting ready with me or walking with my outfit showing — is because I want to show that you don’t have to sacrifice those parts of yourself to be taken seriously. You should be taken seriously no matter what.

    A post shared by Nikita Redkar (@nikitadumptruck).

    According to recent reports, redkar: On Mondays, I have a researcher and we go through the topics that people are talking about on social media. We pull up some news sites and see what the significant stories are, and we leave some room for breaking news throughout the week.

    It has been revealed that my week is [split] between videos [on topics] that the general public is talking about, and videos that are just interesting to me. That’s how I stay sane in this business. I’m lucky to have the flexibility of doing that. My researcher combs through news sites and research papers and compiles all that information for me, then I put together a script.

    Redkar: It’s definitely my favorite color, but it’s like the chicken and the egg — I don’t know if I liked it before I was doing this.

    In a recent development, I pick whatever outfit I feel cute in. In getting ready with me videos, I start with a completely bare face, so at least the outfit has to be giving a little bit.

    Industry observers note that tameez: Tell me about the Get Ready with Me videos. How do you decide what’s a GRWM and what’s a walking video?

    Redkar: It’s like: What am I comfortable screaming out in the streets versus what do I need to keep at home? Some topics require more seriousness; if it does, I can do the GRWM for that. But if it’s something [less serious], I can be walking my dog or have on some ridiculous outfit.

    According to recent reports, redkar: If I get a fact wrong, I’ll do a follow-up video. It’s rare that I’ve gotten a fact wrong because between me and my researcher, that’s two levels of checks before something hits the internet.

    Industry observers note that for one video, I didn’t factually get it wrong, but I should have included more of the story. It was about the Ugandan dictator Idi Amin and how Indians were expelled from Uganda, which is kind of how we got both Zohran Mamdani and Charli XCX [living in the U.S.], because both of their parents were part of the group that was expelled. I disregarded the racism that local Ugandans faced because of the Indians. I just focused on the expulsion and I framed Indians as the victims.

    A lot of people in the comments were like, “Hey, like, you really should have said this other part too.” I just deleted that video, because I didn’t want this to spread and only give half of the story.

    Redkar: My favorite video in recent memory was about girls on the first date, how we’re all so vigilant these days about dating men. I had so much fun doing it because I was talking about how life is affected by politics, instead of just politics. I think that video did really well because a lot of people connected to it.

    According to recent reports, last year I did a video that I called “How we went from Brat Summer to Hitler Winter” and talked about the hedonism of the 2024 summer and the fascism that followed. I related it to the Roaring 20s transitioning to the Great Depression to the World War. I incorporated a lot of pop culture [references].

    A post shared by Nikita Redkar (@nikitadumptruck).

    Sources indicate that redkar: Constantly. I posted a video about the Cornell professor who invented the term sexual harassment. I thought it was so interesting and timely, but it did not do well at all. The problem with content creation is sometimes you can’t tell if people didn’t like a video or if you’re being shadow banned.

    Sources indicate that redkar: I really love Liz Plank. She’s @feministabulous on Instagram. I love her coverage and how she leans into current conversations in pop culture.

    I really like Charles McBryde. He’s not talking about just news — he’s very foreign policy-focused as well.

    @MissEatingGood on Instagram is a great explainer of what’s going on and the historical context.

    According to recent reports, redkar: Just finding ways to work together. I think there is so much benefit in that. I know countless creators who take a journalist’s article and dissect it down. Maybe [the journalists] should be the ones doing that.

    I would happily pair up with journalists and teach them the ins and outs of content creation and how to make a short-form video article that’s also attention-grabbing. That’s just the reality; people are on social media, everyone’s attention span is shot, which sucks. We could try to fix that, but at this moment, we’re not fixing it. It’s really helpful to go on social media and talk [about your reporting] because journalists work hard on their articles.

    Creators [should] take more time. We rush way too much. It’s not our fault, because these platforms reward you for making content more frequently and punish you if you take a few days off. [Not rushing] sucks, but what can you do? It’s better than putting incorrect, or rushed, or incomplete information out there.
